Sterile Neutrino Self-Interactions in
Cosmology: From Dark Matter

to the Baryon Asymmetry

Dissertation

zur Erlangung des Doktorgrades
der Fakultät für Mathematik und Physik der

Albert-Ludwigs-Universität
Freiburg im Breisgau

vorgelegt von

María Isabel Dias Astros

September 2025



Dekan: Prof. Dr. Michael Růžička
Referent: JProf. Dr. Stefan Vogl
Korreferent: Prof. Dr. Heidi Rzehak

Tag der mündlichen Prüfung: 12.12.2025



ABSTRACT

Sterile neutrinos represent a compelling and well-motivated extension of the Standard
Model, capable of addressing fundamental open questions such as the origin of dark
matter and the baryon asymmetry of the Universe. However, the minimal scenarios for
sterile neutrino dark matter and freeze-in leptogenesis face significant challenges. On
the one hand, keV-scale sterile neutrino dark matter produced through oscillations via
the Dodelson–Widrow mechanism is ruled out by a combination of X-ray searches and
structure formation constraints. On the other hand, the minimal freeze-in leptogenesis
scenario requires a high degree of degeneracy among the right-handed neutrinos, mo-
tivating the exploration of alternative frameworks. To address these limitations, this
thesis investigates the role of sterile neutrino self-interactions in both contexts.
In the dark matter study, we consider sterile neutrinos interacting via a singlet scalar, the
latter with masses ranging from a few keV to a few GeV. These new interactions enable
a self-accelerating production of sterile neutrinos: by allowing the sterile sector to draw
additional energy from the active sector, the resulting sterile neutrino abundance can be
significantly boosted compared to the vanilla Dodelson–Widrow scenario for the same
mixing angle. Within this framework, we identify several distinct production regimes
exhibiting diverse phenomenology, from partial thermalization for low and intermediate
mediator masses to resonant production for heavier mediators. We demonstrate that
significant regions of parameter space open up, highlighting promising regions for future
observations.
The second study, focusing on freeze-in leptogenesis, considers a pair of sterile neutrino
flavours with self-interactions mediated by a singlet scalar via a Yukawa-like coupling.
The new interactions modify the dynamics in two key ways: they lead to an additional
rate of production and destruction of the sterile neutrinos and to the generation of a new
contribution to the effective potential. Assuming that the Yukawa and mass matrices are
not diagonal in the same basis, we find that the new contributions to the sterile effective
potential can enhance the produced baryon asymmetry by several orders of magnitude,
substantially relaxing the mass degeneracy constraints of the minimal scenario.

iii





ZUSAMMENFASSUNG

Sterile Neutrinos stellen eine überzeugende und gut begründete Erweiterung des Stan-
dardmodells dar, mit der grundlegende offene Fragen wie der Ursprung der Dunklen Ma-
terie und die Baryon-Asymmetrie des Universums beantwortet werden können. Die mini-
malen Szenarien für sterile Neutrino als Dunkle Materie und Freeze-in-Leptogenese ste-
hen jedoch vor erheblichen Herausforderungen. Einerseits wird sterile Neutrino-Dunkle
Materie im keV-Bereich, die durch Oszillationen über den Dodelson-Widrow-Mechanismus
erzeugt wird, durch eine Kombination aus der Suche nach anormaler Röntgenstrahlung
und Beobachtungen der großräumige Struktur des Universums ausgeschlossen. Anderer-
seits erfordert das minimale Szenario der Freeze-in-Leptogenese einen hohen Grad an
Entartung unter den rechtshändigen Neutrinos, was die Erforschung alternativer Szena-
rien motiviert. Um diese Einschränkungen zu überwinden, untersucht diese Arbeit die
Rolle der Selbstwechselwirkungen steriler Neutrinos in beiden Kontexten.
In der Dunkle-Materie-Studie betrachten wir sterile Neutrinos, die über ein Singlet-
Skalar interagieren, wobei letzteres Massen im Bereich von einigen keV bis zu einigen
GeV aufweist. Diese neuen Wechselwirkungen ermöglichen eine sich selbst beschleuni-
gende Produktion steriler Neutrinos: Indem der sterile Sektor zusätzliche Energie aus
dem aktiven Sektor beziehen kann, lässt sich die resultierende sterile Neutrino-Anteil
im Vergleich zum klassischen Dodelson-Widrow-Szenario für denselben Mischungswinkel
deutlich steigern. In diesem Rahmen identifizieren wir mehrere unterschiedliche Produk-
tionsregime, die eine vielfältige Phänomenologie aufweisen, von partieller Thermalisie-
rung bei niedrigen und mittleren Mediatorenmassen bis hin zu resonanter Produktion bei
schwereren Mediatoren. Wir zeigen, dass sich bedeutende Bereiche des Parameterraums
eröffnen, und zeigen vielversprechende Bereiche für zukünftige Beobachtungen auf.
Die zweite Studie, die sich auf die Freeze-in-Leptogenese konzentriert, betrachtet ein Paar
von sterilen Neutrinos mit Selbstwechselwirkungen, die durch einen Singlet-Skalar über
eine Yukawa-ähnliche Kopplung vermittelt werden. Die neuen Wechselwirkungen verän-
dern die Dynamik in zweierlei Hinsicht: Sie führen zu einer zusätzlichen Produktions-
und Annihilationsrate der sterilen Neutrinos und zur Erzeugung eines neuen Beitrags
zum effektiven Potential. Unter der Annahme, dass die Yukawa- und Massenmatrizen
in derselben Basis nicht diagonal sind, stellen wir fest, dass die neuen Beiträge zum
sterilen effektiven Potential die produzierte Baryon-Asymmetrie um mehrere Größen-
ordnungen verstärken können, wodurch die Einschränkungen an die Massendifferenzen
des Minimal-Szenarios erheblich gelockert werden.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS

There are so many people I am grateful to, without whom this thesis would not have
been possible.
First and foremost, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to my supervisor, Stefan
Vogl, for being an exceptional guide throughout this journey. When Andreas Trautner
told me that working under your supervision would be incredible, he was absolutely
right. Your support, encouragement, and inspiration have made this PhD experience
truly rewarding. I could not have asked for a better mentor.
To all my family, especially my parents and siblings, who have shaped me and supported
me through every step of my life. I can never repay your unconditional love. A special
thanks to my sister Astrid, whose presence and care sustained me even in the darkest
times.
To my partners in crime — and in suffering — Selina, Julian, and Clara: you made
every day brighter, and your company in the office kept me sane. Without you, office
809 would never have been the same.
To all the members, old and new, of the 7th and 8th floors of the physics highrise who
shared this PhD journey with me: Stefan D., Mathieu, Max S., Jo, Sebastian, the Joses,
Robin, Heidi, Simone, Martin, Jan S., Jonas, Max R., Yannsito, Tim E., Robin B.,
Julian, Clara, and Selina. Thank you for all the interesting conversations, both about
physics and life, and for helping me discover, among other things, who would win in a
battle between a tiger and a bear.
To the Joses, for reading my dreadful first manuscript with such care and for not com-
plaining too much about it.
To my old friends — Alan, Gustavo, Aristides, Jeinny, Kufis, Francisco and Mireia —
who have been with me through different stages of life. You have seen me in moments
of overwhelming panic and stress, but also witnessed my growth into the person I am
today. This thesis is just another challenge I have tackled, and I look forward to sharing
future moments of panic and triumph with you.
And to the (not so) new ones — Miguel, David, Esti, Eduardo, Aranza, Anna, the Joses,
Julian, and Selina — who entered in the latest seasons of my life only to make the story
even better.
All of you have become my family in Germany and abroad.

1 INTRODUCTION

1 Introduction

Even though the Standard Model of Particle Physics stands as one of the most successful
scientific theories ever developed, especially after the discovery of the Higgs boson in
2012, it still falls short of providing a final, all-encompassing description of fundamental
physics. The list of open problems is extensive: from conceptual puzzles concerning
the naturalness of the Standard Model — such as the hierarchy problem, the strong
CP problem, and the hierarchical pattern of fermion masses and mixings — to pressing
phenomenological challenges, including the origin of neutrino masses, the nature of dark
matter, and the mechanism behind the baryon asymmetry of the Universe. Considerable
effort has been devoted in recent years to addressing these issues, both experimentally
and theoretically. Among the various clues pointing toward new physics, neutrinos stand
out as a particularly compelling case.

Neutrino oscillations, firmly established in 1998 by the Super-Kamiokande experi-
ment, are widely regarded as the first direct experimental evidence that the Standard
Model is incomplete. It is therefore not surprising that neutrinos offer exceptional po-
tential as a window into extensions of the Standard Model capable of addressing many
of its shortcomings. The fact that neutrinos oscillate, and thus possess mass, unam-
biguously requires physics beyond the Standard Model. One well-motivated extension
involves sterile neutrinos, i.e. hypothetical fermions that are singlets under the Standard
Model gauge group. Sterile neutrinos appear in many theoretical frameworks that aim to
tackle one or more of the Standard Model’s open problems. For example, they provide a
natural mechanism for generating small active neutrino masses via seesaw models. Even
more intriguingly, they are also promising candidates for dark matter and may play a
role in explaining the baryon asymmetry of the Universe. However, the sterile neutrino
properties required to solve each of these problems, in terms of mass scale and coupling
strength, are generally different. This points toward scenarios with multiple sterile neu-
trino species, each contributing to a different aspect of the puzzle, rather than a single
particle explaining all three phenomena simultaneously.

One particularly interesting case is that of keV-scale sterile neutrinos, which are
well-suited as dark matter candidates. The simplest realization of sterile neutrino dark
matter is a freeze-in scenario in which sterile neutrinos are produced via their tiny mixing
with the active neutrinos. In this case, each active neutrino has a small probability
of oscillating into a sterile state, with the dynamics determined entirely by just two
parameters: the sterile neutrino mass and the active–sterile mixing angle. This minimal
setup is highly predictive, but it faces severe observational constraints. In fact, the region
of parameter space where such a model can produce the full observed dark matter relic
abundance is now largely excluded by a combination of X-ray searches and structure
formation bounds, motivating the exploration of non-minimal production mechanisms
or additional interactions.

On the other hand, heavier sterile neutrinos appear in theories of leptogenesis, which
aim to explain the origin of the baryon asymmetry of the Universe. Such models are
especially compelling because they arise naturally in scenarios that also account for

1



the smallness of the active neutrino masses. For sterile neutrino masses well above
the electroweak scale, the baryon asymmetry can be generated through their out-of-
equilibrium decays in the early Universe. Alternatively, for masses of only a few GeV,
the asymmetry can be produced via CP -violating oscillations in a freeze-in framework.
However, the simplest implementation of freeze-in leptogenesis often requires a significant
mass degeneracy between the heavy neutrino states to account for the observed baryon
asymmetry.

To address the limitations of these minimal scenarios, this thesis investigates the ef-
fects of introducing self-interactions among sterile neutrinos, mediated by a singlet scalar
field, in the contexts of sterile neutrino dark matter and freeze-in leptogenesis. In the
dark matter study, we consider a setup with a single sterile neutrino and one singlet
scalar mediator. We then explore a wide range of sterile neutrino and mediator masses,
identifying multiple production regimes, each characterized by distinct and rich phe-
nomenology. This allows us to pinpoint regions of parameter space where the observed
dark matter relic abundance can be achieved while simultaneously evading stringent
constraints from X-ray observations and structure-formation data [1].

In the context of freeze-in leptogenesis, we investigate two GeV-scale sterile neutrinos
interacting through scalar-mediated self-interactions, allowing for a fully general struc-
ture of the Yukawa couplings. We show that these self-interactions can substantially
modify the dynamics of the system, thereby alleviating the stringent mass-degeneracy
requirement that characterizes the minimal freeze-in leptogenesis scenario. Our analysis
is restricted to the oscillatory regime [2]. This work opens promising new avenues for
exploring extensions of freeze-in leptogenesis.

The thesis is organized as follows. In Chapter 2, we provide a general overview of ster-
ile neutrinos and their role in neutrino oscillations and the generation of neutrino masses.
Chapter 3 presents a theoretical introduction to cosmology, the dark matter problem,
various models of sterile neutrino dark matter, and their corresponding phenomenology.
Chapter 5 discusses the baryon asymmetry of the Universe with a focus on leptogenesis
theories. Chapters 4 and 6 contain the author’s original studies on extensions of minimal
sterile neutrino dark matter and freeze-in leptogenesis models with self-interacting ster-
ile neutrinos, forming the core of this thesis. Finally, Chapter 7 presents the conclusions.

Conventions and notation

In this thesis, we adopt natural units, i.e. c = ~ = kB ≡ 1, unless stated otherwise.
Additionally, we employ the metric signature (+,−,−,−).

2 INTRODUCTION TO STERILE NEUTRINOS

2 Introduction to sterile neutrinos
Being the only fermions in the Standard Model (SM) without color or electromagnetic
charge, neutrinos hold a unique and compelling potential to reveal physics beyond the
Standard Model (BSM). This potential was brought into sharp focus more than three
decades ago, when the Kamiokande collaboration [3, 4] reported a deficit of atmospheric
muon neutrinos. This unexpected result sparked discussions within the physics com-
munity about the possibility of neutrino oscillations and, by extension, the existence of
nonzero neutrino masses. A few years later, the Super–Kamiokande collaboration [5]
provided strong statistical evidence that not only confirmed the deficit in the expected
neutrino flux, but also demonstrated its dependence on the neutrino path length and
energy, precisely as predicted by the framework of neutrino oscillations. The discovery of
neutrino oscillations and the confirmation of nonzero neutrino masses is now recognized
as one of the first direct indications of physics BSM, a breakthrough that earned the
2015 Nobel Prize in Physics.

One of the simplest frameworks to explain both neutrino masses and their extreme
lightness involves the existence of sterile neutrinos. Introduced initially to account for
neutrino masses, sterile neutrinos were later realized to have broader implications, poten-
tially addressing a variety of phenomena beyond neutrino physics. This chapter provides
a concise overview of neutrino oscillations and explores the role of sterile neutrinos in
generating a mass term for the active neutrinos.

The chapter is organized as follows. In Sec. 2.1, we give a brief overview of neutrinos
in the SM. Sec. 2.2 discusses the role of sterile neutrinos in generating neutrino masses,
with a focus on seesaw models. Finally, Sec 2.3 delves into neutrino oscillations in both
vacuum and matter.

2.1 Active neutrinos

First postulated by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930, neutrinos have since become an essential
part of our fundamental understanding of nature. Within the SM, neutrinos are the
only fermions that carry neither electromagnetic nor color charge, i.e. they are singlets
under the subgroup SU(3)C ×U(1)EM. There are three flavours of neutrinos, each asso-
ciated with a generation of charged leptons. In the SM, left-handed leptons and quarks
transform as doublets under the fundamental representation of SU(2)L. The neutrinos
appear in the left-handed lepton doublets alongside their charged lepton counterparts,
while the up- and down-type quarks form analogous left-handed quark doublets. The

2.3 The physics of neutrino oscillations

If SM neutrinos have mass, lepton flavour is not conserved during neutrino propagation,
leading to the phenomenon known as neutrino oscillations [16–19]. In the SM, neutrinos
are produced and detected through weak interactions in specific flavour eigenstates,
typically labeled νe, νµ and ντ . These states form the flavour (or interaction) basis. In
general, however, the neutrino mass matrix is not diagonal in this basis, so the mass
eigenstates — i.e. the freely propagating states — denoted as ν1, ν2, . . . , νm with m ≥ 3,
differ from the flavour eigenstates. As a result, a neutrino created in a given flavour can
later be detected as another, with the transition probability oscillating over time. In
what follows, we briefly review the underlying physics of this phenomenon.

3 STERILE NEUTRINOS AS DARK MATTER

3 Sterile neutrinos as dark matter
As discussed in the previous chapter, sterile neutrinos provide a natural framework to
explain both the origin and the smallness of active neutrino masses. In addition, sterile
neutrinos in the keV mass range — being neutral, massive, and long-lived particles —
are well-motivated dark matter candidates (see, e.g. [37–41] for comprehensive reviews).
This chapter focuses on the topic of sterile neutrino dark matter (SNDM) and it
is organized as follows. Section 3.1 begins with a general overview of the dark matter
problem, introducing key cosmological concepts, summarizing the historical evidence,
and outlining common production mechanisms and leading candidates. Section 3.2 is
dedicated to deriving the Boltzmann equation governing the sterile neutrino evolution in
the early Universe, while Sections 3.3 and 3.4 present two specific production scenarios.
Finally, Sec. 3.5 discusses the phenomenology and current observational constraints on
SNDM.

3.1 The dark matter problem

Dark Matter (DM) is arguably one of the most widely debated topics in modern particle
physics. Since Einstein’s formulation of General Relativity (GR) in 1915 and the sub-
sequent theoretical and observational developments, our understanding of the history of
the Universe has grown significantly. We now have a good picture of the key events that
shaped the cosmos, tracing its evolution back to about 10−34 seconds after the Big Bang.
However, although several observations have settled that dark matter and dark energy
are the dominant contributions to the energy density of the Universe, their fundamental
description remains unknown.

Understanding DM requires a solid grasp of the cosmological framework in which it
evolves. The following section provides a brief overview of modern cosmology, setting
the stage for the subsequent discussion of DM.

3.1.1 Modern cosmology in a nutshell

The fundamental picture of modern cosmology relies on the Big Bang scenario, describing
the Universe as a system that evolved from a highly dense state around 13.8 billion years
ago. There are plenty of cosmology books to study the topic in detail. In particular
[42, 43] were used for this introduction. Building a cosmological model requires of three
ingredients:

• A metric gµν describing the geometry of the Universe.

• An equation of state characterising the properties of the energy content in the
Universe.

• Einstein field equations relating the two above.

Let us go through each of these ingredients at a time. At first glance, specifying a
metric that describes the entire Universe may seem like a daunting task. However,

Having laid out the key ideas of cosmology — including the Friedmann equations,
the continuity equation, and the expansion of the Universe — we are now equipped to
follow the Universe’s evolution. These principles will let us piece together a timeline,
from the first instants after the Big Bang to the vast cosmic structures we see today,

3.1.2 A one-minute recap of 13.8 billion years of cosmic history

Our model of the early Universe is conceptually simple: we extrapolate known physics up
to the Planck epoch. Beyond this point, our current theories break down. Attempting
to evolve the Universe all the way to t = 0 leads to a singularity with a(0) = 0, the
so-called Big Bang singularity. Although our understanding of the earliest moments is
limited, there is broad consensus among cosmologists that the Universe underwent a
brief but dramatic phase of accelerated expansion known as inflation [46]. During the
inflationary epoch, the Universe was driven to a highly homogeneous state with (almost)
zero spatial curvature. Inflation ended with the transfer of its energy to the SM sector
(and possibly to BSM particles) through a process known as reheating [47, 48]. Reheating
marked the beginning of the hot Big Bang in which the Universe became filled with a
hot and dense plasma of relativistic particles in thermal equilibrium10. From the end
of reheating onwards, the particles in the SM plasma remained in equilibrium as long
as their interaction rates could compete with the expansion of the Universe. When the
rate of expansion H exceeded the rate at which interactions among particles occurred,
the species decoupled from the thermal bath. This departure from equilibrium, as we
will see later, played a crucial role in shaping the Universe we observe today.

With the hot Big Bang in place, the Universe followed a well-defined thermal history.
As the Universe cooled down due to the expansion, at T ∼ 100GeV, particles in the SM
acquired masses through the Higgs mechanism during the electroweak phase transition
(EWPhT). At T ∼ 150MeV, a second key transition occurred when quarks, which at
high energies had behaved as free particles, became confined into mesons and baryons.
This is known as the Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) phase transition. When the
temperature dropped to T ∼ 1MeV, the weak interactions could no longer compete
with the cosmic expansion, causing neutrinos to decouple from the plasma. They then
free streamed, forming the cosmic neutrino background [50]. Shortly afterwards, the
temperature fell below the electron mass, triggering electron–positron annihilations. The
entropy from these annihilations was then transferred to the photons, but not to the
already decoupled neutrinos. This resulted in the photons being “heated” with respect
to the neutrinos. Indeed, after e+e−-annihilation, the neutrino temperature became
lower than the photon temperature by a factor of (4/11)1/3 (see Fig. 3.2).

Following neutrino decoupling and e+e−-annihilation, the Universe continued to ex-
pand and cool, setting the stage for the next key milestones in its thermal history. About
three minutes after the Big Bang, at temperatures of a few hundred keV — below the

3.1.3 Experimental evidence for dark matter

At the end of Sec. 3.1.1, we discussed how, in the era of precision cosmology, the den-
sity parameters of the Universe’s various energy components can now be measured with
percent-level accuracy. At first sight one might assume, aside from the fact that we
do not really know what dark energy is, that our cosmological model is well estab-
lished. Nonetheless, the baryonic content of the Universe, i.e. the amount of visible
non-relativistic matter, amounts to just Ωb = 0.0493(6). This is only a small fraction of
the energy density allocated to matter. In fact, ordinary matter makes up only about
16% of the matter content of the Universe, while the remaining ∼ 84% is in the form
of dark matter. The nature of DM is an ongoing puzzle that has persisted for almost
a century (see e.g. [55]). In the following, we provide a brief historical overview and
highlight the most compelling evidence supporting the existence of DM.

It is widely agreed upon that the swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky was the first one
to provide robust evidence for the existence of DM [56]. In 1933, Zwicky studied the
redshifts of several galaxy clusters using data published two years earlier by Hubble and
Humanson [57]. Particularly interesting was the velocity dispersion of galaxies in the
Coma Cluster. Using the virial theorem12 applied to a system of 800 galaxies, each with
a mass of 109 solar masses and distributed within a sphere of 106 light-years, Zwicky
estimated the velocity dispersion to be approximately 80 km/s. This value contrasted
sharply with the observed average line-of-sight velocities of about 1000 km/s. From this
discrepancy, he therefore concluded that a greater amount of matter than that visible
in the cluster was required to account for the observations. This unseen component is
what we call DM nowadays. Similar conclusions for the Virgo cluster were put forward
only three years later by Sinclair Smith [58] and, in the following decades, numerous
studies addressed the problem of the light-to-mass ratio in galaxy clusters. Yet, during
this period, the DM hypothesis was neither accepted nor completely disregarded.

The breakthrough finally came in the 1970’s with the observations of galaxy rotation
curves by Ford and Rubin [59, 60]. Galaxy rotation curves map the orbital velocities
of stars and gas as a function of their distance from the galactic center. In Newtonian

3.1.4 Features of dark matter candidates

The observational evidence discussed in the previous section not only establishes the
presence of DM in the Universe but also constrains the properties it must have. Building
on these insights, below we outline the key characteristics that a viable dark matter
candidate should satisfy [76].

• Appropriate relic density: As required by the Planck data [45], the DM relic
abundance is Ωh2 = 0.1200(12). Any viable DM model must, therefore, feature a
production mechanism that yields this abundance16.

• Stable: The lifetime of DM particles must be at least comparable to the age of the
Universe; otherwise DM cannot fulfill its role in structure formation and current
astrophysical observations [77].

• Non-relativistic: In standard theory of structure formation, DM is required to
be cold (or at most warm), i.e. its constituents must become non-relativistic well
before the era of matter domination. If DM had remained relativistic by this
epoch, density perturbations would have been erased on scales smaller than the
particle’s free-streaming length, contradicting observational data. In contrast, N-
body simulations for cold dark matter (CDM) seem to be in agreement with a wide
range of observations of the large-scale structures that we observe today [78].

3.1.5 Equilibrium thermodynamics

Having outlined the key properties that any viable DM candidate must satisfy, the nat-

Universe17. To this end, we need to introduce some concepts of equilibrium thermody-

3.1.7 Popular dark matter candidates

Having discussed some of the mechanisms by which DM can achieve its relic abundance
— via freeze-out or freeze-in — we can now consider specific particle candidates that
could realize these scenarios. As discussed in Sec. 3.1.4, a viable DM candidate must
satisfy several key properties: (i) stability over cosmological timescales, (ii) darkness,
(iii) collisionlessness, (iv) coldness, (v) the ability to produce the correct relic density,
and (vi) consistency with a broad range of observational constraints. We now turn to
the main DM candidates that meet these requirements.

• Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs): WIMPs are among the
most well-studied thermal dark matter candidates, typically with masses ranging
between a few GeV and a few TeV. WIMPs are produced through freeze-out in the
early Universe and can be embedded in a wide range of theoretical frameworks. No-
table examples include supersymmetry (SUSY) [89–91], two Higgs doublet models
[92, 93], theories with extra dimensions [94], “little Higgs” models [95, 96], techni-
color and composite Higgs theories [97, 98], as well as a plethora of models featuring
Higgs or neutral vector boson portals. Over the past decades, an extensive exper-
imental effort has been dedicated to the pursuit of WIMPs employing different
detection strategies. Among these, direct detection experiments play a crucial role
by searching for nuclear recoils induced by DM–nuclei elastic scatterings. Leading
experiments in this field include LZ [99], PandaX-4T [100], XENONnT [101] and
DarkSide-50 [102]. Altogether, these searches have put stringent upper constraints
on the DM–nucleon scattering cross section, particularly for WIMP masses be-
tween 10 GeV and 10 TeV. Additionally, indirect detection experiments search for
DM annihilations or decays into detectable particles across various cosmic environ-
ments. In this context, gamma-ray observatories such as Fermi-LAT [103], HESS
[104], MAGIC [105] and VERITAS [106] provide the most stringent bounds. While
WIMPs remain a key focus of current experimental efforts, the lack of signals has
driven the community to leave no stone unturned in the search for DM, exploring
a broader range of alternative candidates.

• Sterile neutrinos: It should come as no surprise that the protagonists of this
thesis, sterile neutrinos, can be candidates for freeze-in DM. The following sections
are dedicated to exploring SNDM in detail22.

Other compelling candidates arise from non-thermal production mechanisms:

• Axions and axion-like particles: Axions are a class of light bosonic DM can-
didates23, with the QCD axion standing out as one of the most well-motivated,

cosmology.

23See e.g. [107, 108] for a detailed review of axions in cosmology.

34



3 STERILE NEUTRINOS AS DARK MATTER

particularly for its role in (dynamically) solving the long-standing strong CP prob-
lem [109, 110]. The QCD axion arises as a pseudo–Nambu–Goldstone boson from
the spontaneous breaking of a new global U(1)PQ “Peccei–Quinn” symmetry. A
common feature of these light bosons is that their coupling to the SM is suppressed
by the energy scale fa associated with the broken symmetry. If this scale is very
large, then the axions interact very weakly with the visible sector. In particu-
lar, the QCD axion acquires a tiny mass, approximately ma ≈ Λ2

QCD/fa, where
ΛQCD ∼ O(100MeV) is the characteristic energy of the QCD phase transition.
This typically results in a QCD axion mass in the range 10−12 eV . ma . 10−2 eV.
Axion-like-particles (ALPs), by contrast, can be much lighter, with masses as low
as 10−22 eV [111–114]. ALPs can be produced non-thermally in different ways,
including decays of topological defects [115, 116] and the misalignment mecha-
nism [117–119]. In recent years, a variety of strategies have been employed to
search for ALPs, both directly and indirectly. For instance, stringent constraints
on the ALP–photon coupling have been established through observations of star
lifetimes and energy loss rates in supernovae [120]. On the direct detection front,
experiments such as IAXO [121], CAST [122], ALPS [123], and ADMX [124] are
exploring potential photon–axion conversions in strong magnetic fields. Hopefully,
upcoming experiments will further explore and expand the parameter space of ALP
dark matter.

• Primordial black holes (PBHs): While most discussions on DM focus on par-
ticle candidates, non-particle alternatives remain compelling. Among these, PBHs
are hypothesized to have formed from the gravitational collapse of primordial den-
sity fluctuations in the early Universe [125, 126]. Unlike astrophysical black holes,
which form much later from stellar evolution, PBHs could have originated during
the era of radiation domination. A variety of studies [127–134] have constrained
the allowed mass range for PBHs to constitute the entirety of DM. The viable
window spans roughly the asteroidal-to-sublunar scale, from 1017 to 1023 g (see
e.g. [135] for a detailed review).

The list above is by no means exhaustive, as DM could constitute only one component
of a richer, more complex dark sector with its own particles and interactions [136–138].
The phenomenology of such hidden sectors can be particularly diverse, opening the
door to features such as dark matter self-interactions or even more exotic scenarios,
including dynamical dark matter [139]. Regardless of its true nature, the search for DM
— both through innovative experimental efforts and through the continual development
of theoretical frameworks — remains one of the most active and enduring pursuits in
modern physics.

3.3 The minimal Dodelson–Widrow scenario

The effective treatment developed above provides a practical framework for describing
sterile neutrino production in the early Universe. We now turn to specific applications of
this framework. As first proposed in [140] by Dodelson and Widrow (DW), the simplest
mechanism for producing SNDM in the early Universe relies on oscillations driven by
the mixing of at least one active neutrino with a sterile species. The concept is straight-
forward: each active neutrino produced in the early Universe via weak interactions can
oscillate and has a small probability of converting into a sterile state. This process will
continue until the weak interactions decouple at about T ∼ 1MeV, at which point the
relic abundance of sterile neutrinos remains unchanged. The dynamics of this produc-
tion mechanism are described by Eq. (3.2.5) where one may neglect the fs term on the
right-hand side under the assumption that the initial abundance of sterile neutrinos is
zero and that it remains small throughout due to the tiny mixing angles.

3.5 Bounds and phenomenology of sterile neutrino dark matter

As we have seen in the last section, the DW and Shi–Fuller mechanisms provide clear

3.5.3 Phase-space restrictions

The X-ray limits discussed above primarily constrain the mixing angle between active
and sterile neutrinos. To fully map the viable parameter space of SNDM, however,
it is also necessary to account for constraints on their mass. Since sterile neutrinos are
fermions, they are subject to the Tremaine–Gunn bound [180]. This bound arises directly
from a fundamental principle: the Pauli exclusion principle. The Pauli principle simply
states that no more than one fermion can occupy a given elementary volume of phase
space. Consequently, if DM is fermionic, its phase-space density within a galaxy cannot
exceed that of a fully degenerate Fermi gas. The most stringent constraints, which
exclude sterile neutrinos with masses smaller than O(100 eV), come from observations
of dSphs in the Milky Way [181]. The precise numerical values depend on the specific
set of dSphs considered and on how the phase-space density of DM particles is inferred
from observations26. As we will see in the following, additional probes can impose even
more stringent lower bounds on the mass of SNDM.

3.5.4 Free streaming

Besides phase-space and decay constraints, the viability of sterile neutrinos as DM also
depends on their kinematic properties. As discussed in Sec. 3.1.4, a suitable DM particle
must be sufficiently cold, meaning that it becomes non-relativistic well before the epoch
of matter–radiation equality. Sterile neutrinos, however, are typically produced (and
decouple) while still relativistic and are considered as warm dark matter candidates.
The free-streaming behaviour of WDM has significant implications for the formation of
cosmic structures, which we now turn to examine.

Small aside on thermal warm dark matter: Our current cosmological model,
ΛCDM, which assumes a cold DM component, successfully explains the large-scale struc-
ture of the Universe down to scales of ∼ 1Mpc (corresponding to the typical spacing
between galaxies). It also provides a solid framework for understanding galaxy formation
within DM halos, reproducing detailed galactic properties, including their abundance,
clustering, morphologies and their evolution over time through numerical simulations
[184–186]. However, on scales below ∼ 1Mpc, ΛCDM faces challenges in matching
observations. These so-called small-scale problems include: 1) the missing satellites
problem [187, 188], 2) the cusp-core problem [189, 190], and 3) the too-big-to-fail prob-
lem [191]. These issues raise the question of whether improved modelling of baryonic
physics — such as gas cooling, star formation, and supernova feedback — is sufficient, or
if modifications to the ΛCDM paradigm itself are required27. Among the popular alter-
natives are warm and interacting dark matter models. Beyond its potential to address
small-scale structure issues, WDM is particularly compelling because it provides an al-
ternative to CDM with distinctive effects on structure formation at scales that could be
probed by near-future observations.

quasars29. Lyman-α observations are very useful because they can probe structures at
scales ∼ 0.1 − 1Mpc and redshifts between 2 and 4. These are precisely the scales

is the so called one-dimensional flux power spectrum30 and it is obtained from direct
measurements of the transmitted flux along the line-of-sight to distant sources.

Once measured, the flux power spectrum exhibits a complex dependence on cos-
mological parameters and the underlying matter power spectrum. Consequently, it is
not possible to directly disentangle the contributions of individual parameters from the
observed flux alone. To facilitate meaningful comparisons with cosmological models, hy-
drodynamical simulations are therefore required [183]. These simulations allow for the
generation of mock Lyman-α forest data under different DM scenarios, which can then
be systematically compared to actual observations. By performing such comparisons,
one can infer constraints on the free-streaming length λfs, which in turn can be trans-
lated into lower bounds on the mass of the DM particle itself. Over the past several
years, multiple analyses employing different methods and datasets have been conducted,

4 SELF-INTERACTING STERILE NEUTRINO DARK MATTER

4 Self-interacting sterile neutrino dark matter
As we have seen in the previous chapter, sterile neutrinos are natural candidates for
DM. In particular, the minimal scenario of oscillation-driven production via the DW
mechanism is appealing due to its simplicity and predictivity. However, as discussed
previously and illustrated in Fig. 3.9, current observational constraints exclude the entire
parameter space in which the vanilla DW mechanism could account for all of the observed
DM relic abundance. Despite this limitation, SNDM remains a very economical and
compelling framework, motivating a variety of alternative production scenarios that
have been proposed in recent years. Besides the Shi–Fuller mechanism [159] discussed in
Sec. 3.4, these new ideas include, for instance, active neutrino self-interactions [202–204],
decays of SM singlet scalars [205–207], and dark entropy production [208], among others.
In this chapter, we explore an alternative framework incorporating sterile neutrino self-
interactions. This idea has already been explored in opposing regimes in [209, 210]. On
the one hand, the authors of [209], building upon an earlier proposal in [211], examine
the light mediator limit. In that context, a simplified treatment of the Boltzmann
equation is adopted, neglecting oscillation-driven effects, yet yielding promising results.
Conversely, [210] investigates the heavy mediator regime, employing a full treatment
of the Boltzmann equation and leading to strong conclusions regarding the resonant
production of sterile neutrinos driven by self-interactions. Here, we extend these studies
by systematically exploring a broad range of mediator masses, from a few keV up to
several GeV. The results of this study have been published in [1].

The remainder of this chapter is organized as follows. In Sec. 4.1, we introduce the
model of sterile neutrino self-interactions and highlight the key differences compared to
the vanilla DW production mechanism. Sec. 4.2 outlines several useful approximations
that simplify the analysis. In Sec. 4.3, we classify the different production regimes and
discuss the relevant dynamics in each case. Sec. 4.4 is devoted to the phenomenology of
the model, where we confront the parameter space with observational constraints from
X-ray searches and structure formation data. Finally, in Sec. 4.5, we summarize our
findings and present our concluding remarks.

4.3 Production regimes

Despite the simplifications made in the last section, Eqs. (4.2.9) must still be solved
numerically. As in the vanilla DW scenario, at high temperatures the active rate and
potential — both scaling as T 5 — suppress active–sterile oscillations, so that any initial
population of DW-produced sterile neutrinos only arises once the temperature drops
below a few GeV. This DW production peaks around T ∼ 100MeV and effectively ceases
as weak interactions fall out of equilibrium. Therefore, to determine the abundance of
sterile neutrinos in the early universe, it is sufficient to integrate the Boltzmann equation
starting at temperatures of a few GeV.

Introducing sterile neutrino self-interactions, however, modifies the evolution in mul-
tiple ways. Importantly, in this case the production of sterile neutrinos is determined
by the interplay of three key quantities: (i) the vacuum oscillation frequency ω, (ii) the
sterile rate Γs, and (iii) the sterile potential Vs. As we will see in the remainder of this
chapter, this interplay is crucial and will allow us to identify different regimes in the
production of νs.

4.4 The parameter space

4.4 The parameter space

In this section, we explore the viable parameter space of the model and confront it with
existing observational constraints. As discussed in Sec. 3.5.2, sterile neutrinos constitute
a form of decaying DM, with the most phenomenologically relevant decay channel being
the one-loop radiative process (see Fig. 3.8). The X-ray photons produced in such decays
are actively searched for by current and upcoming X-ray telescopes, providing the most
stringent constraints on SNDM produced via the DW mechanism. The same constraints
apply in our scenario: the radiative decay rate is determined solely by the sterile neutrino
mass and mixing angle, independent of the details of the production mechanism. We
therefore adopt the X-ray limits from [172, 174, 177, 179], which translate into an upper
limit on the mixing angle as a function of the sterile neutrino mass.

In addition, structure formation bounds must be taken into account. As discussed in
Sec. 3.5.4, WDM candidates can suppress the formation of structures on scales smaller
than their free-streaming length. While non-resonantly produced sterile neutrinos are
not thermal WDM particles, their effect on structure formation is qualitatively simi-
lar. In fact, there exists a direct mapping between the mass of a thermal WDM relic
and that of sterile neutrinos produced via the DW mechanism that yields an equiva-
lent suppression in the matter power spectrum (see Eq. (3.5.8)). In our scenario, sterile
neutrinos are likewise produced while still relativistic, and therefore also suppress the
growth of small-scale structures. Accurately evaluating the resulting limits, however,
requires detailed cosmological simulations which lie beyond the scope of this work. In-
stead, we adopt a simplified, approximate approach. Bounds on WDM from structure
formation are usually reported in terms of the smallest mass allowed for a particle with
a thermal distribution and vanishing chemical potential. These bounds are translated
from direct constraints on λfs derived from the simulations. Equivalently, one can write
the bounds in terms of the root-mean-square velocity vrms (see Eq. (3.5.5)) of the DM

4.5 Summary

Although sterile neutrinos are well-motivated and promising DM candidates, the simplest
realization of SNDM is already ruled out by current observational constraints. For this
reason, there is significant interest in exploring possibilities beyond the canonical DW
scenario. In this chapter, we have focused on a scenario in which sterile neutrinos have
a new self-interaction mediated by a singlet scalar with a mass in the range of a few keV
to a few GeV. The phenomena that affect the production of DM in this setup are rich,
giving rise to different production regimes that are primarily determined by the mediator
mass and the Yukawa coupling. Delimiting these regimes is challenging, especially since
the system’s evolution also depends on the mixing angle and is generally nonlinear. As a
useful rule of thumb, however, we can identify four characteristic regimes provided that
the combination of y and the mixing angle is such that DM is not overproduced:

1. For mediator masses mφ . 100MeV, the system is well described by the simplified
ansatz of the Boltzmann equation given in Eq. (4.3.1). In this regime, the effects
of potentials and quantum damping are negligible, while the interaction rate dom-
inates the dynamics. Since the DW mechanism and the new scalar interactions
occur at well-separated temperature scales, the problem can be effectively factor-
ized into two independent phases. For sufficiently large Yukawa couplings, the
system can also undergo partial thermalization which provides an extra boost to
the relic density.

2. For mediator masses greater than approximately 100 MeV, the production by DW
and the production sourced by self-interactions overlap in time. In this regime, the
full Boltzmann equation must be solved numerically in order to track the evolution
of the sterile population. We find, however, that for masses up to mφ ∼ 800MeV
the mediator is not heavy enough to support the development of resonances in the
effective mixing angle. Quantum damping can nevertheless play a significant role,
particularly for neutrinos at the high-energy end of the spectrum.

3. For mφ ∼ 1GeV the effective mixing angle can develop resonances for some mo-
mentum modes. In this case, however, the on-shell part of the scattering rate is
typically large, so the quantum damping term dominates the transition probability,
with 〈Pm〉 ∝ 1/Γ2

t . As a result, the production of sterile neutrinos is regulated.

4. Finally, for very heavy mediators with mφ & 3GeV, the system reaches a regime
where resonances are no longer effectively regulated. In this case, there is a sharp
transition between underproduction and overproduction of DM.

In all cases except the last, the observed DM abundance can be produced. Crucially,
this can occur for mixing angles that are orders of magnitude smaller than those needed
in the vanilla DW scenario. This opens up large new regions of parameter space where
SNDM remains viable. While parts of this parameter space are already excluded by

5 Sterile neutrinos and their role in leptogenesis

In the previous two chapters, we explored the potential of sterile neutrinos as DM can-
didates, demonstrating in particular how their self-interactions could enable them to
account for the observed relic abundance. Yet, sterile neutrinos may have implications
beyond the dark sector. In this chapter, we turn to a different but equally fundamental
question: how sterile neutrinos may contribute to explaining the Baryon Asymmetry of
the Universe (BAU).

This chapter is organized as follows. In Sec. 5.1, we introduce the general problem
of the baryon asymmetry and review the conditions that any viable model must satisfy
to generate it, along with an overview of the most prominent theoretical frameworks.
In Sec. 5.2, we discuss the relation between baryon and lepton asymmetries. Sec. 5.3
presents the parametrization of seesaw models commonly employed in leptogenesis sce-
narios, while Sec. 5.4 provides a brief review of thermal leptogenesis. Finally, in Sec. 5.5,
we give an overview of minimal freeze-in leptogenesis.

5.1 The baryon asymmetry of the Universe

The problem of the BAU stems from a simple but striking observation: all known cosmic
structures are composed of matter, with no substantial amounts of antimatter detected
anywhere in the Universe. Antimatter is observed only in trace amounts, primarily in
cosmic rays from both our galaxy and distant sources, but its abundance is extremely
small. For instance, antiprotons appear at a relative abundance of roughly 10−4 com-
pared to protons [222], consistent with them being secondary products of cosmic-ray
collisions with interstellar matter.

This evidence strongly indicates that significant amounts of antimatter do not exist
in our local cosmic neighborhood. Furthermore, if large, separate regions of matter and
antimatter existed, annihilations at their boundaries would produce a diffuse gamma-ray
background. Yet, no such signal has been observed. In fact, analyses suggest that only
negligible amounts of antimatter could exist on scales of order ∼ 20Mpc, the typical size
of galaxy clusters [223]. Collectively, these observations point to a pronounced matter–
antimatter imbalance in the Universe. Understanding the origin of this asymmetry
remains one of the central challenges in modern cosmology and particle physics.

The BAU is usually quantified in two different ways [7, 45, 224], i.e. by the baryon-
to-photon ratio

this process are collectively known as theories of baryogenesis. We refer the reader to
more complete reviews on baryogenesis, e.g. [225–228], on which most of the rest of this
section is based.

5.1.1 Sakharov Conditions

In 1967, Sakharov pointed out that any model capable of generating the BAU in a
dynamical way must satisfy three conditions [229]: (i) baryon number violation, (ii) C
and CP violation and, (iii) departure from thermal equilibrium. We now examine each
of these conditions in more detail.

• C and CP violation
The violation of charge conjugation (C) and the combined symmetry of charge
conjugation and parity (CP ) may not seem immediately essential in the context
of baryogenesis. However, if either C or CP were conserved, processes involving
baryons would occur at the same rate as their corresponding processes involving
antibaryons. The result would be that no net baryon asymmetry could be gener-
ated.
To see this more explicitly, consider a schematic process i → f , where i and f
denote some initial and final states, respectively. If C was conserved, the probabil-
ity for the process i→ f would be equal to that of the charge-conjugated process
ī → f̄ . Since the baryon number of f is equal in magnitude but opposite in sign
to that of f̄ , the net contribution to the baryon number cancels, resulting in an
overall zero asymmetry.
Moreover, because of the CPT theorem, CP invariance implies invariance under
time reversal T . This means that the rate for the process i(xi,pi, si) → f(xj ,pj , sj)

Surprisingly, it seems that the SM contains all the necessary ingredients for baryogene-

First, the amount of CP violation arising from the CKM matrix is many orders of mag-

5.1.2 Models of baryogenesis

As noted in the previous section, explaining the origin of the BAU requires new physics
that extends the SM in at least two ways: (i) introducing new sources of CP violation
and (ii) providing a suitable mechanism for departure from thermal equilibrium. In this
section, we list some possible extensions of the SM that lead to successful baryogenesis.

• Grand Unified Theories (GUTs): GUTs provide a natural framework for ex-
plaining the BAU [249–251]. These theories aim to unify the fundamental interac-
tions under a single gauge symmetry, within which the SM gauge structure appears
as a subgroup (for a review, see e.g. [252]). The central idea is that at high ener-
gies, this unified gauge symmetry is spontaneously broken — possibly through a
series of intermediate steps — ultimately yielding the SM gauge structure observed
at low energies. In GUTs, baryon number violation arises naturally from the fact
that quarks and leptons are embedded within the same representation of the uni-
fied group. Moreover, additional sources of CP violation are easily accommodated
due to the richer flavour structure and the presence of new complex phases beyond
those in the SM. Finally, the departure from equilibrium condition required for
baryogenesis can be satisfied through the out-of-equilibrium decays of heavy GUT
bosons in the early Universe. Despite their appeal, GUT models face significant
phenomenological challenges, most notably the prediction of proton decay. The
non-observation of this process imposes stringent lower bounds on the masses of

78



5 STERILE NEUTRINOS AND THEIR ROLE IN LEPTOGENESIS

the decaying bosons and, by extension, on the reheating temperature of the Uni-
verse after inflation. Possible solutions to these issues have been explored in, e.g.
[253, 254].

• Electroweak baryogenesis: Electroweak baryogenesis comprises a class of mod-
els where the departure from thermal equilibrium is provided by the electroweak
phase transition. The SM, in principle, falls within this class. However, as briefly
discussed in the last part of Sec. 5.1.1 generating the BAU during the standard
‘vanilla’ EWPhT requires of a strong first-order phase transition, which does not
occur in the SM44. As a result, models of electroweak baryogenesis typically in-
volve modifications to the scalar potential of the SM to alter the nature of the
phase transition. Among the most widely studied scenarios are supersymmetric
extensions, such as the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) [255–
259], as well as non-supersymmetric frameworks like the two-Higgs-doublet model
(2HDM) [260–262].

• Leptogenesis: Originally proposed by Fukugita and Yanagida [263], leptogenesis
is a mechanism in which the observed BAU is generated from a lepton asymmetry.
The remainder of this chapter is devoted to a detailed exploration of leptogenesis
and the role played by sterile neutrinos in this process.

5.2 Relating the baryon and lepton asymmetries

5.4 Thermal leptogenesis

Let us now turn our attention to a concrete realization of leptogenesis. As discussed
in Sec. 5.2, the fact that B − L is conserved in the SM opens up the possibility for the
baryon asymmetry to be generated from a lepton asymmetry. The underlying idea is
that, if an asymmetry in lepton number is generated, sphaleron transitions will reprocess
it and partially convert it into a baryon asymmetry (see Eq. (5.2.11)). This mechanism,
however, relies on the creation of an initial lepton imbalance, which necessarily requires
the existence of lepton-number violation. In the seesaw framework introduced in Sec. 2.2,
such violation arises naturally through the Majorana mass terms of right-handed neu-
trinos. In this way, leptogenesis thus establishes a non-trivial connection between two
seemingly unrelated phenomena: (i) the existence of the BAU, and (ii) the masses and
mixing of neutrinos.

Thermal leptogenesis belongs to the class of models of baryogenesis where the asym-
metry is created from the out-of-equilibrium decay of heavy particles, as in GUT scenar-
ios. Its original implementation is based on the type-I seesaw mechanism (see Sec. 2.2),
and the asymmetry is generated by three thermally-produced right-handed heavy neu-
trinos N1, N2 and N3. Indeed, in thermal leptogenesis, the three Sakharov conditions
are naturally satisfied: (i) lepton number is violated by the Majorana mass terms, (ii)
new sources of CP violation are introduced in the neutrino Yukawa couplings and (iii)
the departure from thermal equilibrium is achieved by the out-of-equilibrium decay of
the heavy neutrinos.

In essence, thermal leptogenesis occurs in three key steps: first, the heavy sterile
neutrinos are thermally produced in equilibrium at very high temperatures; second, as

Note that, while we have so far discussed oscillations and equilibration as if they were
independent, it is in fact their interplay that determines the dynamical regime of lepto-

several distinct oscillation and equilibration time scales, each associated with a different
flavour. If the slowest oscillation time is much shorter than the fastest equilibration time,
leptogenesis proceeds in the so-called oscillatory regime. In this scenario, the neutrinos
undergo several oscillations before equilibrating, with the bulk of the asymmetry gener-

there is a clear separation of scales, between the time of asymmetry generation at zosc
and the time when the washout processes become efficient at zeq, i.e. zosc � zeq. This
separation of scales allows us to treat both processes independently, and an expansion
in the couplings |F ∗FT| can be performed to estimate the asymmetry analytically (see
Eq. (5.5.7)).

Conversely, if the fastest equilibration time is much shorter than the slowest oscillation
time, i.e. zeq � zosc, the system enters the overdamped regime. In this case, a perturba-
tive expansion in the couplings is no longer valid, although analytic approximations can
still be constructed (see e.g. [288, 293, 294] for more details).

6 Freeze-in leptogenesis with self-interacting sterile neu-
trinos

As discussed in the previous chapter, leptogenesis has become a highly active area of
research, especially following the discovery of neutrino oscillations, which established
that neutrinos are massive and mix between flavours. It remains a compelling frame-
work, as it provides a natural and generic mechanism for generating the BAU within
type-I seesaw models, providing a link between the smallness of neutrino masses and
the matter–antimatter imbalance in the Universe. Among the various realizations of
leptogenesis, scenarios involving relatively light sterile neutrinos, potentially accessible
to current and/or future experiments, are very attractive. These include, for example,
the neutrino minimal standard model (νMSM) [286, 287, 305–307] and resonant lepto-
genesis [308, 309]. In particular, the νMSM employs the ARS mechanism discussed in
the previous chapter and offers a unified framework to address both the BAU and the
dark matter problem through the addition of three right-handed neutrinos to the SM.

However, the fact that the net asymmetry produced in the vanilla ARS mechanism
is inversely proportional to the mass splitting between the heavy sterile states, implies
that successful leptogenesis requires a high degree of mass degeneracy. This introduces
a fine-tuning problem, which is one of the main limitations of the vanilla scenario. Fur-
thermore, while lighter sterile neutrinos are kinematically accessible in many current
and near-future experiments, this advantage is counteracted by the small values of the
Yukawa couplings, typically of order O(10−7), which are extremely hard to probe experi-
mentally [310]. To address these issues, and further motivated by the possible occurrence
of additional fields in nature, interactions among sterile neutrinos have gained increas-
ing attention (see e.g. [311, 312]). Certainly, new interactions in the sterile sector could
enhance the prospects for future detection. Nonetheless, studies have shown that intro-
ducing interactions which bring the right-handed neutrinos earlier into equilibrium can
actually suppress the generated BAU and, in the best-case scenarios, lead only to an
O(1) enhancement relative to the minimal ARS framework [311, 312]. Further extensions
were studied in, e.g. [313–315].

In this chapter, we focus on the first issue, namely the mass degeneracy required in the
vanilla ARS mechanism. Our main goal is to investigate whether self-interactions among
sterile neutrinos can alleviate the degree of fine-tuning in the mass splitting typically
needed for successful leptogenesis. To this end, we consider a setup involving two sterile
neutrinos interacting via a scalar singlet. While our framework shares similarities with
the models considered in [311, 312], we allow for a more general structure in the Yukawa
couplings than the ones considered in those studies. The results presented here are
published in [2].

This chapter is organized as follows. In Sec. 6.1, we introduce the model and highlight
the key differences from the vanilla ARS mechanism. We also explain how the new
interactions enter the QKE. In Sec. 6.2, we present numerical solutions to the problem at
hand. To provide context and deeper insight, Sec. 6.3 derives an approximate analytical
solution in the oscillatory regime and emphasizes the main differences compared to the

6.1 Scalar-extended ARS

In this work, we extend the simple type-I seesaw mechanism given in Eq. (2.2.6) including
sterile neutrino self-interactions. These interactions are mediated by a singlet scalar φ
that we assume to be in thermal equilibrium with the SM plasma at the temperatures
that are relevant for leptogenesis. The interaction Lagrangian reads

−Lint = YijN̄iNjφ, (6.1.1)

with i, j = 1, 2 labelling sterile neutrino flavours and Y denoting a 2×2 real and symmet-
ric Yukawa matrix. Note that, if the field φ acquired a vev, the term in Eq. (6.1.1) would
generate masses for the sterile neutrinos. In the case in which this would be the only
source of neutrino masses, the Yukawa matrix Y and the heavy neutrino mass matrix M
would be diagonal in the same basis. Here, we remain agnostic about the precise origin
of neutrino masses, allowing for a more general scenario in which M and Y are treated as
independent. This is the crucial distinction between our approach and previous studies
on scalar extensions for ARS leptogenesis where, either a diagonal Yukawa matrix was
assumed [311], or the neutrino masses were generated directly through the vev of the
scalar field φ [312]. As it will become clear in the following, the fact that M and Y are
diagonal in different bases leads to an enhancement of the generated BAU via thermal
effects in the dispersion relation of the sterile neutrinos.

The interaction term in Eq. (6.1.1) modifies the minimal ARS leptogenesis framework
in two key ways: (i) it introduces an additional contribution to the thermal potential of
the sterile neutrinos, and (ii) it opens up new channels for the production and annihila-
tion of right-handed neutrinos. We now examine these effects in more detail.

6.4 Closing remarks

Sterile neutrinos provide a simple yet well-motivated extension of the SM, with the
intriguing potential to address several longstanding puzzles in particle physics and cos-
mology. Especially, their role in leptogenesis offers a compelling connection between the
observed BAU and the phenomena of neutrino masses and oscillations. If the masses of
the right-handed neutrinos lie below the electroweak scale, leptogenesis proceeds via the
ARS mechanism. In this scenario, the asymmetry is generated through CP -violating

115



6.4 Closing remarks

oscillations of the heavy neutrinos. Unlike thermal leptogenesis, in the ARS mechanism
the sterile neutrinos remain largely out of equilibrium with the SM plasma until after
electroweak symmetry breaking, effectively acting as a reservoir that hides a fraction of
the lepton number from sphaleron processes. However, generating a sizable asymmetry
in the minimal ARS framework imposes stringent constraints on the system. In par-
ticular, the oscillation timescale, which is set by the mass splitting between the sterile
neutrinos, must not be too short compared to the time of sphaleron freeze-out. This
requirement translates into a strong degeneracy between the sterile neutrinos, such that
O(GeV)-scale neutrinos must have mass differences as small as a few tens of keV. Such a
strong degeneracy, while theoretically possible, motivates the exploration of mechanisms
that could relax this requirement.

In this work, we demonstrate that introducing self-interactions among the sterile neu-
trinos can significantly alleviate this fine-tuning in the mass splitting. Specifically, we
consider a scalar-mediated interaction with Yukawa-like couplings to the sterile neutri-
nos. This new interaction impacts the system in two key ways: (i) it modifies the sterile
neutrinos self-energies through an additional thermal potential and (ii) it opens new
channels for the production and annihilation of neutrinos. Each of these effects intro-
duces a characteristic time scale, which plays a crucial role in determining the evolution
of the asymmetries. Our analysis reveals that, within the oscillatory regime, the sterile
potential dominates the dynamics across a broad region of parameter space. In this
limit, the QKE can be solved analytically and the resulting asymmetry reproduces the
full numerical solution to within a factor of two. Importantly, the presence of the new
interactions can enhance the generated baryon asymmetry by several orders of magni-
tude. This enhancement significantly relaxes the mass splitting constraint present in the
vanilla ARS scenario.

Our results open a promising new direction for exploration within the ARS frame-
work, though further research is necessary to fully investigate the range of possibilities.
In general, this is a complex problem due to the various timescales involved, which can
be hierarchically arranged in different ways. Even in the vanilla scenario, alternative
solutions are known to exist, see, for example, the discussion of the overdamped regime
in [288]. In this work, we did not attempt a systematic exploration of these alternative
regions of parameter space. Understanding the role of self-interactions in such regimes
remains as an open and intriguing question. For the sake of tractability, we also intro-
duced several simplifications to reduce the number of degrees of freedom. For instance,
we focused on the case with equal diagonal Yukawa couplings, Yii = Yjj . The more
general case with Yii 6= Yjj is left for future work. Finally, a comprehensive phenomeno-
logical study would be highly valuable to connect the dynamics of the early Universe
explored here with experimental observables accessible today, e.g. through direct or in-
direct searches for heavy neutrinos (see [283] for a review), or through searches for light
scalars at the LHC.

7 CONCLUSIONS

7 Conclusions

Sterile neutrinos have become a central focus of research, especially following the discov-
ery of neutrino oscillations and the confirmation that neutrinos possess non-zero masses.
They are highly compelling because they offer a minimal and theoretically well-motivated
extension of the SM, with the potential to address several of its shortcomings. Perhaps
the most immediate motivation lies in their ability to naturally explain the smallness
of active neutrino masses via the seesaw mechanism. Beyond this, sterile neutrinos also
open up intriguing possibilities in cosmology. At the keV scale, they constitute promising
DM candidates featuring characteristic astrophysical signatures, while at the GeV scale
and above, their dynamics can give rise to the observed BAU via leptogenesis. In this
thesis, we focused on these two cosmological roles, building on the results published in
[1, 2].

The possibility that sterile neutrinos with masses of order keV could account for the
DM of the Universe was pioneered by Dodelson and Widrow in the 1990s. While this
“vanilla” scenario is extremely appealing in its simplicity, it is now firmly excluded by
observational constraints, from X-ray searches to structure formation data. To overcome
this limitation, in [1] we explored an extended framework where sterile neutrinos feature
self-interactions mediated by a new scalar singlet φ. In our setup, a single sterile flavour
mixes with one active neutrino and couples to φ via a Yukawa-like interaction. The
phenomenology of DM production in this scenario is surprisingly rich. We identified
four distinct production regimes, which are primarily determined by the mass of the
mediator and the strength of the Yukawa coupling. These regimes are: (i) the low mass
regime (mφ . 100MeV), for which the production of sterile neutrinos can be separated
into two phases, i.e. an initial contribution from the vanilla DW mechanism followed by
an additional production phase sourced by the new interactions; (ii) a low-intermediate
regime (100MeV . mφ . 800MeV) where quantum damping due to the new interaction
rate can play an important role; (iii) a high-intermediate regime (1GeV . mφ . 3GeV)
where possible resonances developed in the effective mixing angle are regulated by quan-
tum damping; and (iv) the high mass regime (mφ & 3GeV) for which resonances are
not regulated efficiently and the system becomes fine-tuned. The key takeaway is that
in all these regimes, except the high-mass case, the observed DM relic abundance can be
obtained with mixing angles well below those required in the original DW mechanism.
This substantially enlarges the viable parameter space for SNDM and opens up regions
that could be probed by future astrophysical searches.

Sterile neutrinos can also play a crucial role in leptogenesis, providing a direct link
between the observed BAU and the masses and mixing of neutrinos. For right-handed
neutrinos with masses above the electroweak scale, the asymmetry is generated through
the out-of-equilibrium decays of the heavy neutrinos, a scenario known as thermal lep-
togenesis. In contrast, for sterile neutrinos with masses below the electroweak scale, the
baryon asymmetry arises from CP -violating oscillations of the right-handed states, via
the ARS mechanism. In this minimal ARS setup, however, the generated asymmetry
is inversely proportional to the mass splitting of the sterile sector, meaning that a siz-

117



able asymmetry requires a significant degree of degeneracy between the right-handed
neutrinos. To address this limitation, in [2] we considered a similar extension in which
the sterile neutrinos feature scalar-mediated self-interactions. In our setup, two heavy
sterile states couple to a singlet scalar via a general Yukawa matrix. These new inter-
actions modify the system in two key ways: (i) they introduce an additional correction
to the sterile’s dispersion relation and (ii) they provide additional contributions to the
production and annihilation processes of the sterile states. Focusing on the oscillatory
regime, we found that the sterile potential dominates the dynamics of the system in a
wide portion of parameter space. In this limit, we were able to find an analytical solution
to the generated baryon asymmetry, which agrees with the full numerical solution within
a factor of two. The key result is that the scalar-mediated self-interactions can enhance
the BAU by several orders of magnitude compared to the minimal scenario, substantially
relaxing the fine-tuning required on the mass splitting of the sterile neutrinos.

Several avenues remain open for further exploration. In the context of SNDM, it would
be promising to investigate how the new scalar-mediated interactions affect production
in alternative cosmological scenarios, such as in the presence of primordial lepton asym-
metries, as in the Shi–Fuller mechanism. It is also worth exploring whether the concepts
developed here can be applied to other dark matter models featuring mixing, for example
dark photon scenarios. For the scalar-extended ARS framework, one could study more
general Yukawa structures beyond the symmetric case considered here. The exploration
of other regimes of ARS leptogenesis, including the overdamped regime, is also worth
pursuing. Furthermore, a detailed phenomenological analysis would be interesting to
connect this model with astrophysical observations and particle searches. Finally, it
would be valuable to examine whether insights from both studies could be combined
and whether a unified framework could be developed to highlight deeper connections
between the two cosmological roles of sterile neutrinos.

Overall, the two studies presented in this thesis illustrate that sterile neutrino self-
interactions provide a versatile and compelling extension of the minimal sterile neutrino
framework. By introducing scalar-mediated interactions, we were able to alleviate key
limitations of both the minimal DW dark matter scenario and the freeze-in ARS leptoge-
nesis mechanism. These interactions broaden the range of viable possibilities for sterile
neutrino cosmology, highlighting new directions that may be explored both theoretically
and observationally. We hope that the insights gained here will serve as a basis for future
research, fostering a deeper understanding of the intricate connections between particle
physics and cosmology.

one can also determine nref from the forward scattering amplitude, which changes sign
if there is a resonance in the amplitude. In our case, the resonance is from the s-channel
exchange of φ and one expects the potential to change signs from s < m2

Résumé

Le Modèle Standard a connu d’importants succès au cours de ces dernières an-
nées. Cette théorie s’est prouvée fiable après de fructueuses prédictions, et décrit
parfaitement les interactions à basse énergie. Néanmoins, certaines questions
restent ouvertes. Les neutrinos dans le Modèle Standard (MS) ne subissent pas
le mécanisme de Higgs et ne possèdent donc pas de masses malgré l’observation
de leurs oscillations. De plus, la matière noire ne trouve pas d’explication au sein
du MS. Nous savons que la matière noire représente environ 84% de la densité
de matière de l’univers et qu’elle est composée de matière non-baryonique. Ces
deux problèmes ne sont pas nécessairement décorrélés. Ce manuscrit traite de
l’étude de modèles scotogéniques où matière noire et masse des neutrinos sont
des problématiques intriquées. La masse des neutrinos est radiativement générée
par la secteur sombre au niveau boucle. Pour ce faire, il est nécessaire de faire
appel à de la nouvelle physique. Ainsi nous étendons le MS par des fermions et
des scalaires singlets et doublets, et nous étudions la phénoménologie de viola-
tion de saveurs leptoniques et de matière noire. Cette étude se base sur l’analyse
numérique effectué par l’implémentation d’un Markov Chain Monte Carlo. Nous
montrons également que le modèle scotogénique peut expliquer les récentes obser-
vations du moment magnétique anomal du muon et qu’il peut générer l’asymétrie
baryonique observée.

ABSTRACT

Abstract

The Standard Model (SM) had numerous successes during the past years. This
theory proved itself to be reliable through the success of plethora predictions. It
describes perfectly interactions at low energies. Nevertheless, there are still open
questions. Within the SM, neutrinos are not sensitive to the Higgs mechanism and
thus are massless. However, their oscillations have been observed which indicate
at least two non zero massive states. Moreover, dark matter cannot be explained
within the Standard Model. Dark matter represents about 84% of the matter
density of the Universe and is composed of non-baryonic matter. The two issues
can be entangled. This is the hypothesis made in this manuscript, where neutrino
masses are generated from the dark sector within scotogenic models. The SM is
extended by fermions and scalars in order to study the phenomenology of lepton
flavor violation while generating neutrino masses and providing a viable candidate
for dark matter. The study uses a numerical code based on a Markov Chain
Monte Carlo technique. We tend to explain the anomalous magnetic moment of
the muon as well as the observed baryon asymmetry within scotogenic models.

Résumé détaillé

Comprendre les phénomènes physiques et plus particulièrement la composition
de la matière est un enjeu qui remonte à la Grèce Antique. Dans l’Introduction
nous remontons à Empédocle et sa définition de la matière pour arriver à la dé-
couverte du boson de Higgs. La physique des particules cherche à répondre à
cette question « De quoi le Monde est-il fait ? » pour citer Halzen et Martin
[1]. Après une introduction à l’Histoire de la physique en Europe, le manuscrit se
découpe en trois Chapitres afin de développer au mieux mes travaux de recherches.

Le Chapitre 1 intitulé « Le Modèle Standard » est scindé en deux parties.
La première est une introduction au Modèle Standard (MS). Nous rappelons
quelles sont les particules qui constituent le Modèle Standard et nous portons un
intérêt particulier aux fermions. Pour cela nous développons les unités naturelles
dans lesquels nous travaillons ainsi que les nombres quantiques des leptons et des
quarks. Nous explicitons le mécanisme de Higgs qui permet de générer une masse
aux particules. Pour finir, nous explicitons les interactions avec les fermions, et
nous rappelons le Lagrangien électrofaible.

Dans la seconde partie de ce Chapitre 1, nous développons certaines limites
du Modèle Standard. En effet le Modèle Standard est une très bonne théorie à
faible énergie, mais qui comporte certaines limites. Nous ne détaillons pas toutes
les questions qui se posent aux Modèle Standard, mais uniquement les points
clés que nous tentons de résoudre par la suite. Cette deuxième partie détaille
les motivations des divers projets de recherches menés. La première limite du
Modèle Standard que nous détaillons est la masse des neutrinos. En effet, ces
derniers sont considérés comme possédant une masse nulle dans le MS. Cepen-
dant nous avons observé une oscillation de saveurs des neutrinos ce qui implique
au moins deux états massifs non nuls. Cette section commence par une introduc-
tion sur l’histoire des neutrinos et se poursuit sur leurs oscillations et les états de
masses. Nous décrivons le mécanisme le plus célèbre au-delà du MS pour générer
une masse à ces derniers qui est le mécanisme du SeeSaw. La section suivante
traite de la matière noire. Ce problème est tout d’abord abordé d’un point de
vue historique par les découvertes de l’astronome français Le Verrier. Il y a
historiquement deux façons de palier à un problème de masse manquante: la pre-
mière etant d’ajouter un objet massif, tandis que la seconde consiste à les théories
de la Relativité Générale. Dans ce manuscrit nous ajouterons de la masse à l’aide
de particules massives. La matière noire est un problème largement étudié. C’est
pourquoi il existe une gamme large de candidats à la matière noire. Dans cette
introduction au problème nous énumérons certains candidats et nous développons
particulièrement les WIMPs qui seront notre candidat à la matière noire. Finale-
ment, nous passons en revu les différentes méthodes de détections. La dernière
limite au Modèle Standard que nous abordons dans ce Chapitre 1 est le moment
magnétique anomale. Nous détaillons le processus de calcul du moment magné-
tique anomal de l’électron. Les récentes mesures du moment magnétique anomale
