Le Chapitre 2 intitulé « Modèles Scotogéniques » se base sur les travaux
qui ont mené à la publication [2]. Afin de répondre aux trois limites énoncées
précédemment nous utilisons un modèle scotogénique. Pour fournir une masse
aux neutrinos, un candidat viable à la matière noire et expliquer les tensions dans
les valeurs du moment magnétique anomale du muon, nous étendons le Modèle
Standard. La première partie du Chapitre 2 est une introduction aux modèles
scotogéniques et détaille le premier modèle scotogénique proposé par Ernest Ma.
Le mot ”scotogénique” possède deux racines Grecs. La première, scoto, signifie
sombre tendis que la seconde, genique, signifie générer. C’est un modèle qui va
à la fois générer une masse aux neutrinos et fournir un candidat à la matière
noire. Le premier modèle de Ma étend le MS d’un champ scalaire et de trois
fermions de Majorana. Ainsi une masse radiative est générée aux neutrinos et
deux candidats à la matière noire sont possibles. Le modèle scotogénique peut
étendre le MS par l’ajout d’un nombre différent de fermions et de scalaires, ce
qui créera des topologies différentes. Nous explicitons certaines des topologies
possibles qui sont listées dans [3] et pour la prochaine analyse nous utiliserons
la forme ”T1”. La seconde partie du Chapitre 2 est l’analyse du modèle T1-2A
qui est un modèle scotogénique qui étend le MS de deux singlets, un scalaire et
un fermion, et deux doublets, dont un scalaire et un fermionique. Afin de définir
l’espace des paramètres nous utilisons un code numérique basé sur la technique du
Markov Chain Monte Carlos (MCMC). Pour appliquer le Markov Chain Monte
Carlos, nous devons appliquer diverses contraintes, prenant en compte la masse
du Higgs, la détection directe de matière noire avec les données de XENON1T,
la densité relique de matière noire et les taux d’embranchements de désintégra-
tion qui violent la saveur leptonique comme celle du muon en électron et photon.
Ainsi nous pouvons explorer l’espace des paramètres du modèle. Comme vu dans
la définition du modèle scotogénique, ce dernier doit fournir un candidat à la
matière noire et générer une masse radiative aux neutrinos. Dans le modèle T1-
2A, la première masse des neutrinos m1 est zéro. Pour s’assurer d’obtenir les
masses observées de m2 et m3, nous procédons à la paramétrisation développée
par Casas et Ibarra [4]. Le code numérique imbrique différents codes : le MCMC
en Python, le modèle est codé avec SARAH, le code SPheno qui donne le spectre
de masse à une boucle ainsi que diverses observables comme les désintégrations
qui violent la saveur leptonique et la masse du boson de Higgs, et pour finir
nous utilisons micrOMEGAs pour calculer la densité relique et les sections efficaces
pour la détection directe. Dans la section dédiée aux résultats nous analysons
pourquoi le modèle en question tend à favoriser un candidat à la matière noire
fermionique. Nous remarquons que le candidat fermionique provient principale-
ment du doublet que nous avons introduit. En effet le doublet aura des processus
de co-annihilations plus importants que le singlet ce qui pousse la densité relique

Pour la suite nous nous concentrons sur la leptogenèse.

Dans un premier temps nous calculons l’asymétrie CP . Nous devons choisir
un scénario, et dans notre étude c’est la désintégration de l’un des fermions de Ma-

processus qui peuvent éliminer l’asymétrie. Finalement nous obtenons des points

fournir un candidat viable à la matière noire, générer une masse radiative aux

Chapter 1
The Standard Model
From its formalism to its limitations

This Chapter contains two parts. The first one is a review of the Standard Model
(SM) and its formalism. It is the basis for the notations that the manuscript will
follow. It is also a brief reminder of the generation of fermion masses, and the
Feynman rules.

The second part is focused on current questions that cannot be solved within
the SM. There are more limitations to the Standard Model that those exposed
in this section. However, the main goal of this part is to introduce the different
concepts that will be treated later. To do we give a detailed introduction to neu-
trinos and the mechanisms used in Beyond Standard Model (BSM) frameworks
to generate their masses. Then, a special focus on dark matter (DM) will take
place, with a review of its discovery, the computation of the relic density, and the
different methods that aim to detect it. Finally, a discussion about the anoma-
lous magnetic moment will follow. We choose to describe the electron case first,
which is a textbook case. The BSM contribution to the (g�2)µ will be discussed
later in the Chapter 2.

understanding of the fundamental components of matter has increased. The
classification of these particles is made thanks to the Standard Model. This

II Few limitations of the Standard Model

Despite a plethora of confirmed predictions, the SM cannot explain all the
observed phenomena. In this section we review the few limitations of the SM. The
open questions enumerated in this section are the motivations of this manuscript.
My research work tends to answer these questions within a specific framework. We
review neutrino oscillations, and thus the diverse mechanisms to generate neutrino
masses. Then, a discussion about dark matter will take place, from its discovery
to the different detection methods. Finally, we compute the anomalous magnetic
moment of the electron in the SM, and discuss about the recent discovery on the
(g � 2)µ of the muon.

II.1 A neutrino overview

II.1.1 The History of neutrinos

Radioactivity is the loss of energy of a nucleus by radiation, and has been dis-
covered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel. One of the radioactive decays is the beta
decay, which corresponds to the emission of an energetic electron (or positron)
from a nucleus. In 1930, Pauli emitted the idea of a particle called neutrino
to explain the conservation of momentum and energy in beta decays [17]. The
neutrino contains in its name the information about its electric charge (neutral)
and ”ino” refers to the smallness of its mass. The decay of a neutron in Fermi’s
theory is then n ! p+ e� + ⌫e, with an anti-neutrino due to the conservation of
the lepton number Le. Neutrinos in the Standard Model are massless. However,
we currently know that they have a very small mass. Neutrinos only interact

through weak interactions, which makes it a particle difficult to detect. However,
in 1953 Reines and Cowan published their discovery in Science [18], they de-
tected an electronic anti-neutrino thanks to an experiment based on beta capture
⌫e + p $ n+ e+. The research on neutrinos continues with Lederman, Schwartz,
and Steinberger in 1962 [19]. They showed that another flavor of neutrino existed
with the discovery of a muonic neutrino. They received the Nobel prize for their
discovery. A bit more than a decade later, the tau lepton is discovered and a new
flavor of neutrino is expected to be found. Currently three neutrino flavors have
been experimentally observed as predicted in the SM.

Neutrinos continue to be probed. Despite the success of their discoveries,
they still have unsolved questions. We do not measure directly their masses.
Furthermore, we do not know their nature, if they are Majorana or Dirac particles.
Experiments like the neutrinoless double beta decay try to answer this question.

II.1.2 Neutrino oscillations

The Standard Model is built upon symmetries. One unbroken symmetry is
Ue(1) · Uµ(1) · U⌧ (1) that means lepton number is conserved and should not be
violated in the Standard Model. Nevertheless the Homestake experiment [20],
known as a solar neutrino experiment, showed an important discrepancy between
the expected number of electronic neutrino emitted by the sun (from SM pre-
dictions) and the observed one counted. This problem stayed unsolved for three
decades. At this point, the experiment was questioned and our comprehension of
the solar physics reviewed. Finally in 1998, Super-Kamiokande experiments [21]
revealed flavor changed for atmospheric neutrinos. This idea was first proposed
by Pontecorvo based on Kaon oscillations [22, 23]. The Kaons are mesons com-
posed of the quarks us̄. During the propagation of a pure kaon beam, a kaon
turns into its antiparticle. Then it can return into a kaon and so on during the
propagation. This phenomenon is called oscillation. Then, Maki, Nakagawa and
Sakata proposed the hypothesis that the interaction and propagation eigenstates
are not the same. Neutrino oscillation is not speculation anymore [21, 24, 25, 26]
and implies two consequences. The first one is that they violate lepton flavor.
Furthermore their oscillations is a proof of a massive state. The flavor oscilla-
tion can be observed experimentally. Indeed, if electronic neutrinos are emitted
through beta decay in an accelerator, we observe interactions of muonic or tauic
neutrinos. The neutrinos observed are in flavor eigenstates which is a superpo-
sition of the three masses eigenstates. When neutrinos propagate, the speed of
each of their mass eigenstates is different. This speed difference will change the
flavor state of the neutrinos propagating. This is why their oscillations imply to
have massive sates [27]. This mismatch between flavor and mass eigenstates can

II.2 The Dark Matter problem

II.2.1 When the invisible becomes visible

The questioning about ”what is the world made of?” also takes place in a bigger
picture, at the cosmological scale. The desire of philosophers and scientists to
understand the world was important and independent of the scale. However,
the usual way to proceed was first to describe the fundamental components by
the visible, or through the senses. As seen in the Introduction, Empedocles
started to describe matter with four elements. At a larger scale, Aristotles emitted
a cosmological model, in which the Universe rotates around the Earth. The
Earth was at the center of everything, and the other planets and stars had an
intrinsic movement. The model developed was complex. However, some issues
were unexplained. The planets seemed to slow down and go backward. The
geocentric model had been accepted for a long period of time. Many alternatives
to this theory were emitted, but without success in a religious context where the
inquisition was actively chasing any ideas that could change the world view as it
was proposed by the Catholic Church. I invite the reader to refer to [56] for a
more historical review. Despite the inquisition, Galileo succeeded to change the
cosmological model imposed by Aristotles thanks to his observations. He used
a telescope to observe the sky and saw satellites in orbit over Jupiter. These
observations were invisible with naked eyes. What was at one time invisible,
became visible with new technologies. Such as the matter has been probed, the
sky has known many observations. This was an important revolution of our

Later, Newton provided his famous laws of motion and Universal Gravita-

tion law in 1687 [57]. It was one of the important breakthrough that changed
physics. Then in 1846, the French astronomer Urbain Le Verrier revealed dis-
crepancies between Uranus’ motion and Newton’s laws. At the same time, the
English astronomer John Couch Adams noticed the same issue. Le Verrier emit-
ted the hypothesis of a missing mass, not discovered, that would change Uranus
trajectory. He used the Newton’s laws to compute the theoretical position of this
body, and sent a prediction of its position to Johann Gottfried Galle in Berlin.
The astronomer in Berlin looked for the object at the position Le Verrier com-
puted. Indeed, the astronomers were right and Neptune was then discovered at
the Berlin observatory. It was a marvelous success that corroborated Newton’s
laws. Another observation revealed an anomalous precession of the perihelion of
Mercury. Again it is Le Verrier who noticed this strange phenomenon. It seemed
that this anomaly could be solved with a similar approach. He emitted the idea
of another planet called Vulcan. Nevertheless, this time no planet was discovered
despite numerous observations around Mercury. The mystery had to wait until
1915 and found an explanation with Einstein and the theory of General relativity
[58]. These historical discoveries brought two answers to the missing mass prob-
lem. The first one, is a physical mass, invisible at the moment, perturbing the
motion of objects. With the improvement of technology, the objects responsible
for the gravitation change can be discovered. The second possible way to address
the problem is to rethink the gravitation theory, as Einstein improved the law of
Gravitation published by in 1687 by Newton.

II.2.2 Evidences of the missing mass problem

Galactic rotation curves The first historical evidence of dark matter lies
in the galactic rotation curves. It corresponds to the circular velocity of stars and
gas as a function of their distance from the galactic center. The famous curves in
Figure 1.6 show indubitably the effects of a missing mass. Measurements of the
galactic rotation curves have began in 1930 but at this period the measurements
were limited to the inner galaxies. With the development of radio astronomy and
the 21cm line of Hydrogen, it was possible to probe the outer part of galaxies
as shown on Figure 1.6. If the luminosity is considered to be a correct indicator
of masses for spiral galaxies, we would predict the rotation curves to be as the
dashed ones in Figure 1.6. However, we observe that at distances larger than 104

light years, the velocity does not decrease as expected. The different behaviour
between the plain and dashed curves confirms a discrepancy to the mass to light
ratio. As mentioned in ”A History of Dark Matter” from Bertone and Hooper
[56], Bessel anticipated the issue with mass to light ratio and said:

”But light is no real property of mass. The existence of numberless visible stars
can prove nothing against the evidence of numberless invisible ones.”

is present in much greater amount than luminous matter.”

mass by applying general relativity [62].

II.2.3 Possible candidates for dark matter

As mentioned above with Le Verrier’s story, two possible solutions are proposed
to solve the missing mass problem. The first one is that this anomaly is caused
by massive objects that we cannot detect yet. The second possibility is a mis-
understanding of the theory of gravitation and the solution will be to redefine
the theory. In this manuscript we will not focus on theory of modified gravity.
Nevertheless, the reader can find more information about it in [71, 72]. We are
more interested in particle candidates for dark matter. Other possible candidates
exist, such as primordial black holes for example [73, 74]. A large diversity of can-
didates for dark matter have been studied by theorists. To illustrate the diversity
of dark matter candidate, see Figure 1.8.

Dark matter candidates should satisfy several properties. First, it has to be

stable (or metastable). Second, dark matter is neutral, so no electric charge.
Otherwise it would have interacted with baryonic matter through electroweak
interactions. Dark matter in standard cosmology should be cold. Even if some
theories propose hot or warm dark matter, in this manuscript we will analyse cold
dark matter (CDM) according to ΛCDM model. We recall that cold means that
the dark matter decouples from the thermal bath as a non-relativistic particle.
This hypothesis allows to form small scale structures first. In another scenario,
the first structures will be large and then collapse to create the small ones. How-
ever from the anisotropy measured in the CMB and from the BAO [75, 76] we
know that the small structures were first created. Finally, the last property of
dark matter is to be massive, since we can observe its gravitational effects. We
propose now to review few of the most promising dark matter particle candidates.

Baryonic candidates. First, a legitimate question would be to ask our-
selves if dark matter is not composed of baryonic matter. As mentioned above,
the candidate from SM should be a neutral particle with a long enough life time
to be considered stable. The only particle within the SM satisfying these condi-
tions are neutrinos. However from there small masses, we know they decoupled
from the thermal bath as relativistic particles. This means it would be a hot dark
matter candidate. Relativistic particles would not have been sensitive to singu-
larities created by the inflation, and would have a large free-streaming. The small
structures would not form first. Instead, super galaxies would be formed and then
fragmented to create the smallest structure. Nevertheless this is not what obser-
vations reveal. In fact, we can see that the oldest structure are small. Neutrinos
could account for less than 10% of dark matter. Futhermore, since they are hot
dark matter candidate, they could not compose the total dark matter density. So
the SM neutrinos cannot solve the dark matter problem.

Another possibility to explain dark matter with the SM, would be Massive
Astrophysical Compact Halo Objects (MACHOs). MACHOs are composed of
compact objects less luminous, such as brown dwarfs, black holes, red dwarfs, or
also white dwarfs. Indeed, the amount of observed matter in galaxies represents
only a fraction of the total density of baryonic matter of the Universe known from
the CMB. The idea of less luminous object not detected can be tempting then.
With microlensing there are tight constraints from EROS [77]. Nevertheless, black
holes are still a good candidate. Some theories can combine different candidates,
such as black holes and a particle candidate.

The Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) might be
the most famous candidate for dark matter due to what is called the WIMP
miracle. WIMPs are particles with a mass range between the MeV and TeV. As
their names reveal it, they interact weakly with baryonic matter. These particles
are considered non baryonic dark matter, and this is what we are looking for in
this thesis. WIMPs are cold dark matter candidates, with a simple mechanism of
production [78]. This candidate offer a large phenomenology and can be probed
through the three detection methods detailed in the next section. Furthermore,

not charged under SU(2). These particles couple to the fermions through mass

’sterile’ refers to their neutrality under the weak interaction. Sterile neutrinos are
not stable but their life time is much larger than the age of the Universe. Their
decay gives a specific signature to look for. This candidate is a warm dark matter
candidate and more information can be found in [85, 86].

II.2.4 Dark matter detection

Scientists investigate dark matter both on its theoretical and experimental as-
pects. Dark matter takes many theoretical shapes and experiments have been
developed to understand its nature. In this section we will review the three types
of experiments to probe dark matter. Indeed they are three ways to probe dark
matter depending on which direction we observe the interactions with DM as
shown in Figure 1.9.

Direct Detection consists of observing the recoil of a nucleus caused by a
DM particle, as shown in Figure 1.10. The Xenon experiment [88, 89, 90, 91]
is an underground experiment where a cylinder is filled with Xenon atoms since
they are very stable. No recoil from dark matter candidates has been observed
currently. But the Xenon1T experiment gives a constraint on the dark matter
cross section, giving an upper limit that we will use along this manuscript. A
compilation of different direct detection limits are shown in Figure 1.11. We will
mainly use the Xenon1T limit as well as the projection of the XenonnT limit.

Indirect Detection is the search of an anomalous flux of Standard Model
particles produced by the annihilation of dark matter [95, 96, 97, 98], or its de-
cay if we consider unstable dark matter as the gravitino [99, 100, 101]. The dark
matter annihilation or decay are searched in the Milky Way and in other galaxies.
Dark matter can produce bosons, fermions, and anti-fermions [102]. An anomaly
in the SM flux is an important probe for dark matter.

Moreover, the matter composition of our Universe and the lack of antimatter is
a question that requires new physics. We will discuss more about the matter
antimatter asymmetry in the Chapter 3.

In order to explore possible solution to the limitations described above, we
extend the Standard Model with new particles in a scotogenic framework.

Chapter 2

Scotogenic models

The main purpose of my research work is to provide a solution to the open
questions mentioned above. To do so we work within a specific framework known
as scotogenic models. First, we will explain how scotogenic models are built.
The first goal of scotogenic models is to generate neutrino masses and provide
a viable candidate for dark matter. After introducing a specific singlet-doublet
scotogenic model, we will discuss about the phenomenology of dark matter, as well
as lepton flavor violation within this framework. After the study of dark matter
and neutrino, we will focus on leptogenesis, which is a mechanism happening
in the early Universe to create the asymmetry between matter and antimatter.
Finally, in the last Chapter, we will have a look at contributions to the anomalous
magnetic moment happening in this specific framework.

I What is a scotogenic model ?

First, let us define what is exactly a scotogenic model. The term ”scotogenic”
comes also from Ancient Greek. The root ”scoto” means dark and ”genic” gener-
ate. The main idea of a scotogenic model stands in its name. It aims to generate
a radiative mass to neutrinos through the dark sector and to provide a viable
candidate for dark matter at the same time. To do so, the Standard Model is
extended with a certain number of scalars and fermions.

MA MODEL SCOTOGENIC MODEL

The first scotogenic model was developed by Ernest Ma [109]. Ma’s model
extends the Standard Model by three neutral fermions Ni, with i = {1, 2, 3},
and a scalar field ⌘. A Z2 discrete symmetry is imposed to prevent the lightest
particle from decaying and consequently insuring dark matter stability. The new

are even. The difference with a classic seesaw model is this Z2 symmetry. Since
⌘ does not take a vacuum expectation value, and Z2 forbids some interactions,
we do not have a Dirac mass term coupling the SM neutrinos to the Majoranas
Ni. As we focus in the next section on more complex model, we develop some
key details about Ma’s model that will be used after.

Z2 symmetry and thus will be the dark matter candidate. Furthermore, lepton

Ma’s model was the first scotogenic model developed. However this is not
the only one providing a solution to dark matter and neutrino masses. In fact,
various topologies are possible in scotogenic models. Among them, certain have
viable dark matter candidates, whereas others can be excluded by indirect and
direct detection, and also by collider constraints. The different model topologies
are referenced in [3]. Different models have been explored [110, 111, 112]. For
this thesis, the models studied are from the type T1 as shown in Figure 2.3. The
different topologies in Figure 2.3 correspond to the diagrams of neutrino mass
generation within the interaction basis, which means before the EWSB. More
precisely, the first model studied in this manuscript is the T1-2A model. At
our understanding, the T1-2A model is a rather generic and minimal scotogenic
model that extends SM with singlet-doublet particles. The study presented is
based on the work [2].

The lack of neutrino masses in the Standard Model despite the experimental
observations [114] and the absence of a candidate for the cold dark matter [30]

are strong motivation for physics beyond the SM. A scotogenic like model can
bring a solution to these issues. In a scotogenic like model the radiative mass
of the neutrinos are generated by the dark sector. The simplest model was first
developed by Ma [109] as mentioned above. The dark sector and the neutrino
masses are not two distinct issues in these models but they are entangled.

The model T1-2A, first studied in Ref. [115], is an extension of the Standard
Model including viable dark matter candidates as well as the radiative generation
of neutrino masses. In addition, a Z2 symmetry is introduced under which all new
fields are odd while the Standard-Model fields are even. In a sens, this corresponds
to a union of the singlet-doublet scalar [116, 117, 118, 119] and singlet-doublet
fermion [116, 117, 120, 121, 122] extensions. More recently, the model T1-2A has
been studied in Ref. [123], focusing on a scalar dark matter.

The present work aims at providing a more complete analysis of this rather
general framework. In particular, we do not restrict ourselves to the case of
scalar dark matter. Moreover, we include CP -violating phases present in the
PMNS matrix. Finally, we include the coupling of the new fields to the right-
handed leptons, which has been omitted in Ref. [123], as it does not contribute to
the generation of neutrino masses. It may, however, have an impact on observable
related to lepton flavour violation, such as µ ! e� and related processes.

We will consider a scotogenic framework, where the Standard Model is ex-
tended by two Weyl fermion doublets, Ψ1 and Ψ2, a Weyl fermion singlet, F , a
scalar doublet, Φ, and a real scalar singlet, S. These additional fields are assumed
to be singlet under SU(3), and odd under a Z2 symmetry to ensure neutrino mass
generation at the one loop level as well as the stability of the dark matter can-
didate. All Standard Model fields are even under the mirror symmetry. Their
quantum numbers are listed in Table 2.1.

II.5 The Markov Chain Monte Carlo technique

II.5.1 General computational setup

Starting from the input parameters given in the MS-scheme at the scale Q =
m

pole

the one-loop level employing the numerical program SPheno 4.0.4 [124, 125],
where we have implemented the model T1-2A making use of the Mathematica
package SARAH 4.3.14 [126, 127, 128, 129]. This setup is also used to compute
the observables related to lepton-flavour violation and low-energy measurements,
which will be detailed in Sec. II.5.4. The dark matter relic density and the di-
rect detection cross-sections are numerically evaluated using micrOMEGAs 5.0.8
[141, 142, 143, 144, 145, 146], where again the corresponding CalcHEP [147] model
files have been generated using SARAH. The parameter values are communicated
between the two codes using the SLHA file format [134, 135].

In order to efficiently explore the parameter space of the model, we employ
a Markov Chain Monte Carlo [148] scanning technique based on the Metropolis-
Hastings algorithm [149, 150]. In an iterative procedure, the parameter space
exploration is conditioned by a large number of (mostly experimental) constraints,
implemented through the computation of the likelihood associated to a chosen
parameter set. A crucial aspect of this technique is the comparison of prior
and posterior parameter distributions, respectively obtained without and with
imposing the constraints.

The Markov Chain Monte Carlo technique has proven to be a very powerful
technique, especially in the exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces.
Originating from cosmology [151] and astronomy [152], this method has also
been applied in phenomenological studies of supersymmetric extensions of the
Standard Model [153, 154] and the determination of parton distribution functions
[155]. To our knowledge, the present analysis is the first extensive study of a
neutrino-mass model employing the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method.

In the following, we detail the computational details, the corresponding input
parameters, as well as the imposed constraints.

This algorithm aims at randomly exploring the parameter space while increas-
ing the likelihood Ln in an iterative manner. Each Markov chain starts from a
parameter point, which is randomly chosen within the intervals given in Tables
2.3 and 2.2 such that its likelihood is (numerically) different from zero. Then, in
each iteration, random values for the parameters ~✓ are picked in the vicinity of
the previous accepted parameter point. The parameters ~✓ are listed in Table 2.2.
In our study, the new proposed parameter value is chosen according to

For each chosen parameter set, the likelihood Ln+1 is evaluated according
to Eq. (2.51) and compared to the likelihood of the previous iteration Ln. If
Ln+1 > Ln, the point is accepted and the chain will continue from this point.
Otherwise, the new point is accepted with probability

p = Ln+1/Ln . (2.50)

If the point is rejected, a new random point is chosen in the vicinity of point n.
Within this framework, the algorithm can move across larger regions while still
converging to highest likelihood places. This is illustrated in the Figure 2.10.

In typical chains, the likelihood value is supposed to grow significantly before
converging towards a plateau near the global maximum. Because low-likelihood
points generated before the convergence occurs are less relevant, we remove the
first 50 points of the chain (burn-in length). This value has been chosen empiri-
cally by observing the likelihood curve across the chains.

In a high-dimensional parameter space (in the present case: 24 parameters),
the quality of the exploration relies more on the total number of chains than the
individual lengths of the chains themselves. Note that different starting points,
chosen randomly, may lead to different likelihood maximums. For the following
analysis, we have generated a total of 86.100 accepted parameter points stemming
from 246 independent Markov chains.

Dark matter direct detection
Let us finally comment on the dark matter direct detection and its implications

on the model parameter space. We show in the left part of Fig. 2.16 the spin-
independent scattering cross-section of a dark matter particle off a nucleon as a
function of the dark matter mass for each valid parameter point of our Markov
Chain Monte Carlo analysis. Points not satisfying the current limits from the
XENON1T experiment [160] are not shown.

This limit excludes a large part of pseudo-scalar dark matter, the remaining
valid configurations being situated relatively close to the exclusion limit. A large
majority of these points lie within the reach of the XENONnT experiment [157],
meaning that the latter will be able to exclude pseudo-scalar, and thus doublet-
dominated scalar dark matter, in a near future. The scalar dark matter config-
urations allowing smaller scattering cross-sections are mainly singlet-dominated.
This corresponds to the case discussed in Ref. [123].

Coming to fermionic dark matter, as discussed in Sec. II.6.2, the region that
is most densely populated corresponds to the case of doublet-dominated dark

II.7 Conclusion

The “T1-2A” model is a rather general framework of the scotogenic type, pre-
senting a very rich phenomenology. We have presented a complete analysis of the
associated parameter space, taking into account constraints from the Higgs sector,
the neutrino sector, lepton-flavour violating processes, and dark matter. To our
knowledge, this is the first analysis of a scotogenic framework taking into account
the complete parameter space together with such a large variety of constraints.

While neutrino data governs the couplings of the new particles to the left-
handed leptons (gF and gΨ in Eq. (2.19)), the couplings to the right-handed
leptons (gR) are mainly constraint by the decays µ ! e� and µ ! 3e as well as µ�
e conversion rates in nuclei. The dark matter relic density and the direct detection
constrain the mass of the new particles as well as their Yukawa couplings. The
XENONnT projection will have an impact on the dark matter nature by excluding
a large part of parameter space featuring pseudo-scalar dark matter.

Focusing on dark matter phenomenology, contrary to previous publications
focusing on one single dark matter candidate, we have considered all three pos-
sibilities, namely scalar, pseudo-scalar, and fermionic dark matter. The latter
turns out to be preferred in view of the imposed constraints.

Moreover, fermionic dark matter is expected to be doublet-dominated. Our
analysis has shown that in this case, a rather precise mass range of about 1.0 –
1.2 TeV can be expected for the dark matter fermion. In this parameter region,
the correct dark matter relic density is achieved through co-annihilations with
the other fermions, while direct detection constraints can be avoided.

The elements discussed in the present paper may be found in other extensions
of the Standard Model featuring similar ingredients, such as, e.g., the possibility
of fermionic doublet-dominated dark matter.

Finally, our results may be used as a guideline for future specific collider
studies. It is to be noted that results from experimental searches for, e.g., su-
persymmetric partners of the Standard Model particles, may be used to obtain
approximate exclusion limits on the present model. Such a study is, however,
beyond the scope of the present study and left for future work.

I.1 The Universe’s timeline
First let us recap the timeline of the Universe and the major events. The first
one, still speculative, is inflation [167]. The inflationary scenario for the Universe
solves the horizon and flatness problem of standard cosmology. During inflation,
the Universe knows a period of exponential acceleration. Modern cosmology
suggests that it is followed by a period of reheating. We recall that at this period
the interaction rate of particles is very important and particles are in equilibrium
in the thermal bath.

The Universe faced the electroweak phase transition in its early time. It
happened when the temperature drops around 100 GeV. Particles got their masses
through the Higgs mechanism. Moreover if dark matter is a WIMP, which is the
dark matter candidate we explore along this manuscript, then it had frozen-out
at this time. Around temperatures of T ⇠ 150 MeV, the QCD phase transition
occurs. At temperatures of 1 MeV, which corresponds about 1 second in the
Universe life, neutrinos decouple from the thermal bath. It is followed 5 seconds
after, when the temperature is around 500 keV, by electron-positron annihilation.

At this stage, the first elements can be formed and nucleosynthesis occurs.
BBN took place at temperatures of about 100 keV, when deuterium, helium and
lithium nuclei are primarily formed. The next major event in the history of the
Universe happened a long time after, when the temperature drops to 0.75 eV,
with the matter-radiation equality. Then when T ⇠ 0.23 � 0.28 eV, photons
decouple. They were mainly interacting through Thomson scattering e� ! e�.
After decouling, they can have a free streaming in the Universe and thus form
the CMB. When they finally decouple, the first atoms of Helium and Hydrogen
can form.

A period called ”cosmic dark ages” appears after this, since stars did not form
yet, there was no visible light. A more visual timeline is represented in Fig. 3.1.

II Introduction to Baryogenesis

The Universe is mainly composed of dark energy and dark matter, see Figure
3.2. The Universe’s composition has only a small portion dedicated to matter,
and more precisely what is called baryonic matter. By definition, baryonic matter
constitutes the stars, the galaxies, the interstellar medium and mostly all the
matter we can experience. In our quest to answer to ”what the world is made
of?”, matter or what we call baryonic matter, is described by the Standard Model
fermions. Furthermore, talking about the components of matter extends naturally
the discussion to antimatter. Today we clearly observe a net discrepancy between
matter and antimatter. Antimatter is composed of antiparticles. By definition,
antiparticles have the same mass than their partners and a similar decay lifetime.
The main difference lies in the quantum numbers, as they carry a negative baryon
or lepton number, and have an opposite electric charge. As the antimatter enters
in contact with its matter partner, it annihilates and most of the time it gives
two photons, e.g. pp ! ��. Observations [177, 76] show an imbalance between
the number of baryons and antibaryons present in the Universe. However the
CP -symmetry should insure a symmetry between particles and antiparticles. So

For a long time, the main explanation for the baryon asymmetry had been to
say it was an initial condition. It raises two issued. The first one is due to inflation.
If we consider the theory of inflation, then the initial asymmetry imposed before
inflation would have been massively diluted [186, 174, 187]. However, in 1967 [188]
Sakharov emitted the hypothesis to generate dynamically the asymmetry. The
theory behind the mechanism responsible of it, had been studied as Baryogenesis.
Instead of fine tuning the initial conditions of the Universe, Sakharov proposed
a dynamical solution to baryon asymmetry. To generate the asymmetry, three
criteria are necessary [188]:

• first, the baryon number B has to be violated to pass from no baryon
asymmetry to the observed asymmetry,

• then the CP symmetry must be broken,

• and finally, the model should include a deviation of thermal equilibrium.
Indeed, since in chemical equilibrium the quantum numbers as B are con-
served and the asymmetry cannot be generated.

Nevertheless these conditions are present in the SM. Indeed, the CP symmetry is
broken in meson decays [189] for example. The CP symmetry is violated in weak
interactions as it was showed in Wu’s experiment [190]. This symmetry trans-
forms a particle `i into its antiparticle `i. If CP were conserved we would observe
no preference in the final states of decays (`i would have the same probability
than `i to be generated), and then no imbalance between matter and antimatter
would be observed. Moreover baryon number is violated in the SM [191]. How-
ever, it is not possible to generate a baryon asymmetry which will be large enough

Conclusion

Along this thesis we saw that the Standard Model is a deeper attempt to an-
swer the question physicists and philosophers asked since Ancient Greek ”What
is the World made of?” than the description by the four elements. The Standard
Model describes with success the fundamental constituents of matter and their in-
teractions at low energies. Its predictions made it a reliable theory. Nevertheless,
with the advances in technologies, experiments and their precision confronted the
Standard Model to face some limitations. The observations are important probes
for new physics, and the SM need to be extended. Neutrinos are not sensitive to
the Higgs mechanism and are thus massless within the Standard Model. How-
ever, experiments [32, 25, 31] measured neutrino oscillations and their difference
squared mass. The prediction of the SM with QCD corrections to the anomalous
magnetic moment was a stringent success. Nevertheless, new data from Fermilab
on the (g � 2)µ [5] are in tension with SM values. Furthermore, other questions
such as the nature of dark matter, or neither the baryon asymmetry observed
cannot be satisfy within the Standard Model framework [30].

The work from this thesis tends to answer some of the SM limitations. Thus
the Chapter 1 was dedicated to introduce both SM and the limitations we want to
work on. We described the fermion sector of the SM and gave useful information
about analytical computation of amplitudes of Feynman diagrams. The section
about the SM limitations is a review about neutrino properties as their oscillations
in the vacuum, and the Seesaw type-I mechanism to generate them a mass. After a
brief historical introduction to dark matter, we review the different candidates and
its properties. Along this thesis, dark matter is considered to be a be cold, stable,
massive, and neutral particle. Finally we explain the origin of the anomalous
magnetic moment by computed the one from the electron, which is a famous
example.

The Chapter 2 bring viable solutions to some of the SM limitations by working
within a specific framework from the scotogenic type. The scotogenic model aims
to generate neutrino masses from the dark sector, and to provide a candidate
for dark matter. The phenomenology of dark matter candidate is quite large in
this framework, since it can be a fermion, a scalar or a pseudo-scalar. The main
difference with a Seesaw model is the Z2 symmetry under which SM particles
are even and the new particles are odd. From our analysis of two singlet-doublet
scotogenic models, we can answer the limitations mentioned previously. The
analysis was made using the Markov Chain Monte Carlos technique. With this

The first singlet-doublet scotogenic model studied in this manuscript is called

that the couplings are low enough to largely satisfy the upper limits on LFV con-

magnetic moment of the muon, and we need extra degrees of freedom to avoid
tensions between neutrino masses, BR(µ ! e�), and (g � 2)µ. This is why we
extend the T1-2A model with another Majorana singlet.

With the added singlet, we were able to create a hierarchy in the Yukawa
couplings and satisfy the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. Moreover,
it gave another source of CP violation to create the baryon asymmetry. The
decays of the new Majorana fermions are responsible for the matter antimatter
asymmetry, and thus contribute to the leptogenesis mechanism.

Chapter 3 starts with an introduction to the thermal history of the Universe.
Since Leptogenesis occurs in the early stage of the Universe, before electroweak
phase transition, it seemed useful to recall the Universe time line and the needed
quantities for relativistic and non-relativistic particles. Leptogenesis is one of the
possible mechanisms to generate baryogenesis. The theory of baryogenesis was
introduced by Sakharov [188] to dynamically generate the baryon asymmetry. In-
deed the observations from BBN [180, 181, 182, 183, 184] and CMB anisotropies
[177] point towards the same discrepancy between baryons and antibaryons. Us-
ing the Boltzmann equations, we can compute this baryon asymmetry within the
extended T1-2A model. More precisely, we generate a lepton asymmetry that is
then transferred to a baryon asymmetry through sphaleron processes, which con-
serve the B�L asymmetry. The model can generate the observed asymmetry for
some points, while satisfying neutrino masses, LFV and dark matter constraints,
and can also provide the observed contribution to aBSM

abstracts.value: This paper is a non-planar counterpart of the author's earlier work on planar contact structures and topological quantum computation. There the page is planar and all branch points are paired by disjoint liftable arcs, compatibly with the joint eigenlines of the Ising representation and with Calabi-Yau (CY) Stein fillings, those with vanishing first Chern class. Here the page has genus g and connected binding, presented as a simple degree-three cover of the disk. Every maximal system of disjoint liftable arcs has exactly g members and leaves two branch points unused. The half-twist interchanging the two points is not liftable, but its cube is, and lifts to the identity. An integral residue criterion supplies the CY test. A factorization localized on a contact connected sum is automatically CY. Unlike in the planar case, a CY factorization need not be the shortest. Once the fusion channels of the g pairs are fixed, Ising fusion determines the channel of the remaining pair, and braiding acts there only by scalars. Fibonacci fusion can leave that channel undetermined, and the powers of the cube then act by ten distinct relative phases on a single joint eigenspace, while the CY Stein filling stays fixed

titles.title: Non-planar contact structures with Calabi-Yau Fillings and topological quantum computation

abstracts.value: Up to now, the Standard Model (SM) remains confronted with several outstanding issues, including the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe, as well as the masses, oscillations, and hierarchical structure of neutrinos. These challenges are closely tied to the naturalness and stability of the SM, and have motivated numerous proposals for new physics beyond the SM. The BESIII experiment has accumulated the world's largest data samples at the $J/ψ$ and $ψ(3686)$ resonances, providing an ideal environment for probing signatures of physics beyond the SM. This proceeding presents a summary of recent results published by the BESIII Collaboration on the searches for lepton/baryon number violation (LNV/BNV), charged lepton flavor violation (CLFV), and charmonium weak decays.

titles.title: Search for new physics with charm data at BESIII

abstracts.value: We study whether a quantum verifier can find a hidden quantum state by exchanging classical messages with an unbounded prover who knows the state. The verifier has access to a reflection oracle about the target. For a Haar-random $n$-qubit target, we prove that achieving constant average fidelity with the target requires $(q+1)^2(B+1)=Ω(2^n)$, where $q$ is the number of verifier queries and $B$ is the total prover-to-verifier communication. The bound allows arbitrary classical interaction and unrestricted computation between queries. Our proof extends the lower bound of Aaronson and Kuperberg from a single classical proof to an arbitrary classical interaction. As a result, we obtain a quantum-oracle separation of UniqueQMA from QCIP with polynomially many classical messages. In particular, we give a unitary oracle $\mathcal{U}$ such that there exists a language $L\in\mathrm{UniqueQMA}^{\mathcal{U}}$ but $L\notin\mathrm{QCIP}^{\mathcal{U}}$. We further give an oracle construction for a notion known as QMA-QCIP[2] gap problem. This gives average case hardness for a QMA language under classical access to a QCIP[2] decision oracle and is used in establishing negative results on witness encryption and quantum indistinguishability obfuscation.

titles.title: Quantum State Search with Classical Interactive Advice

abstracts.value: In an earlier work, we showed that, in the interaction-dominant setting, coupling the conjugate variables of a subsystem to distinct environment modes drives the subsystem to a maximally mixed state. Here, we extend the study to the full quadratic dynamics of a single-mode subsystem coupled to a two-mode environment, and identify the phase-space mechanism responsible for the asymptotic behavior. By tracking the exact reduced Weyl characteristic and Wigner functions, we demonstrate that they lose their dependence on local phase-space coordinates on every fixed compact region. In free-particle model, this happens for all values of coupling, whereas in the harmonic oscillator model, it happens above a critical value of the coupling. Under a finite-volume and momentum regularization, this behavior corresponds to the reduced subsystem approaching a maximally mixed state.

titles.title: Conjugate measurement-induced evolution towards maximally mixed states in quadratic quantum systems

abstracts.value:
Complex amplitudes can be simulated over real Hilbert spaces by adjoining a two-dimensional real/imaginary degree of freedom. In a multipartite program, however, one globally shared phase tag is not a locality-preserving program transformation: every party would have to act on the same auxiliary system. We recast the distributed real simulation of multipartite quantum mechanics as a syntax-directed compiler into a real misty-state intermediate language. For $n$ parties we give explicit phase-reference codewords $|0\rangle_{P_n}$ and $|1\rangle_{P_n}$ on $n$ local tags and prove that the same real operator $J=XZ$ on any single tag realizes the logical action of multiplication by $i$. If a complex party-local gate is $A=A_R+iA_I$, its real translation is 
\[ \widehat A_j=A_R\otimes I+A_I\otimes J_j, \]
 which acts only on party $j$'s data and local phase tag. We prove an intertwining theorem for arbitrary finite party-local pure-state circuits, exact preservation of computational-basis measurement probabilities, preservation of the run-time interaction graph, and one-rebit-per-party overhead. For the canonical three-party GHZ program, the translation lies entirely inside the ordinary black-and-white misty gate fragment: controlled-$J$ replaces the complex phase operation, while the invariant $J_jJ_k|0\rangle_P=-|0\rangle_P$ transfers the required branch sign. This yields a short correctness proof for all four promised GHZ inputs and explains the earlier 64-path cancellation calculation at a single logical phase-code boundary. We distinguish this program realification problem from the weaker task of finding any real strategy with the same correlations, and state precisely which parts are known real-Hilbert-space simulation and which parts belong to the misty-language compilation layer developed here.

titles.title: Distributed Phase Tags: A Locality-Preserving Realification Compiler for Misty-State Quantum Programs

abstracts.value: We extend the holographic test of entanglement cohomology from $d=2$ to higher-dimensional conformal field theories. For a $d$-dimensional CFT with a spherical entangling region $A$, the vacuum modular Hamiltonian is known explicitly, and the boundary relative entropy of a primary-operator perturbation can be computed via conformal Ward identities. On the bulk side, the perturbation is dual to a scalar field in AdS$_{d+1}$, and the bulk canonical energy is computed using the JLMS relation. We carry out the computation explicitly for $d=3$ and $d=4$ and find that the boundary and bulk results agree at first order in the perturbation, with identical coefficients $κ_d Δ^2 / C_T$, where $κ_3 = π^2/12$ and $κ_4 = 3π^3/16$. The result extends the quantitative verification of the holographic dual of entanglement cohomology beyond the $d=2$ case treated in the companion paper and confirms that the modular Hamiltonian perturbation is the correct holographic image of the first entanglement cohomology class. We discuss the role of the conformal anomaly, the shape of the entanglement wedge, and an outlook on TsT-deformed backgrounds. \keywords{Entanglement entropy \and Cyclic cohomology \and von Neumann algebras \and Holography \and Modular Hamiltonian}

titles.title: Higher-Dimensional Test of the Holographic Dual of Entanglement Cohomology

abstracts.value: We propose an $\mathbf{O}(D,D)$-covariant holographic dictionary for two bulk completions of the Gomis--Ooguri boundary data: Riemannian $AdS_3$ supported by pure NS--NS flux and an everywhere non-Riemannian string Newton--Cartan geometry. An $\mathbf{O}(D,D)$-covariant Codazzi identity yields the boundary conservation law. Both branches share diagonal generalized-metric one-point functions, but only the non-Riemannian branch carries independent normalizable soft hair that couples to long strings without contributing to surface charges or the renormalized on-shell action. Supersymmetric non-Riemannian saddles admit arbitrary chiral Killing-spinor profiles, realizing "supersupersymmetry."

titles.title: Non-Riemannian Holography: Long Strings and Soft Hair

abstracts.value: Although Sn nuclei have long been considered typical spherical nuclei, the $E2$ transitions in neutron-deficient Sn nuclei have posed a puzzle. We argue that their deformability may resolve this issue, based on self-consistent calculations with a semi-realistic interaction. The significant role of the pseudo-spin symmetry, which is attributed to the effects of the tensor force, is also discussed.

titles.title: Deformability of neutron-deficient Sn nuclei studied with semi-realistic interaction

abstracts.value: Accurately characterizing molecular properties and reactivity often requires electronic-structure calculations across an ensemble of molecular geometries. Quantum algorithms that process such ensembles coherently could address this challenge, but they require Hamiltonian block encoding circuits that combine advanced factorization techniques with sublinear scaling in ensemble size. Here, we introduce SVD-THC, which extends tensor hypercontraction to sets of Hamiltonians defined at different nuclear geometries through a singular value decomposition of the ensemble. We use SVD-THC to construct a single multiplexed block encoding circuit for all geometries in an ensemble. We then evaluate the approach on ensembles generated by varying internal rotational coordinates in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane as well as in glycine and alanine dipeptides, corresponding to established model systems for peptide conformational landscapes, with up to 5,184 geometries. Across several resolutions of the internal-coordinate grids, the Toffoli complexity of the resulting circuits grows only weakly with the number of geometries, changing by at most 12% over grids that differ in size by up to 576$\times$. In an energy-thresholding circuit, this yields 35--200$\times$ fewer Toffoli gates than slicing together single-geometry block encodings. This approach could help make coherent processing of molecular geometry ensembles a useful primitive for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

titles.title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians

abstracts.value: Ultraviolet-softened extensions of general relativity can weaken gravity at short distances, whereas a positive Källén--Lehmann spectral density forbids gravity from falling below Newtonian strength. Which property of the mediator must such a weakening sacrifice? For Lorentz-invariant Gaussian mediators coupled linearly to the conserved stress tensor, we formulate three independent interferometric conditions that jointly imply this bound: visibility is never amplified, decoherence is fixed by the energy radiated by the difference source, and no interferometer responds to a later one. At tree level, the three ghost prescriptions of quadratic gravity each violate exactly one: negative-norm ghosts amplify coherence, negative-energy ghosts decohere without positive energy transfer from the difference source, and a time-symmetric fakeon response produces advanced fringe shifts. Any universal short-distance weakening of gravity therefore certifies that its mediator violates one of these conditions, and the observables proposed to certify quantum gravity become consistency tests of its ultraviolet completion.

titles.title: Interferometric trilemma for ultraviolet-softened gravity

abstracts.value: We study quark matter at high isospin asymmetry in the limit of vanishing baryon density, a state of matter governed by the condensation of charged pions. In the weak-coupling limit, this state of matter can be reliably described by conventional perturbative methods where a trivial ground state is assumed. However, since the condensate of charged pions generates a gap in the excitation spectrum of the quarks with a non-perturbative dependence on the strong coupling, corrections to the results from conventional perturbative methods arise. This situation is very reminiscent of the one encountered in isospin-symmetric quark matter at high baryon densities which is expected to be a color superconductor. In the present work, we calculate the thermodynamic properties of superfluid quark matter at high isospin asymmetry, zero temperature, and zero baryon density at next-to-leading order (NLO) in the coupling in the presence of a finite gap. We work in the limit of two massless quark flavors and further assume that the gap is small compared to the isospin chemical potential. Similar to the situation in color-superconducting quark matter at high baryon densities, we find that the gap-induced corrections lead to an increase of the pressure and the speed of sound above their values obtained for non-superfluid quark matter. Notably, starting from asymptotically high isospin asymmetries, these corrections lead to a systematic change of the slope of the speed of sound when the isospin asymmetry is decreased. We compare our results with recent lattice QCD and Dyson-Schwinger equation studies and find good agreement in the regimes where these methods are applicable.

titles.title: Thermodynamics of two-flavor isospin-asymmetric superfluid quark matter at next-to-leading order

abstracts.value: We develop a systematic method to compute the subsystem fidelity and Rényi fidelity in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) from the operator product expansion of twist operators, and apply it to the subsystem quantum Bhattacharyya distance (BD) and Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance (RBD). We validate the method against exact results in the free massless fermion and boson theories, and then use it to compute the BD and RBD in holographic CFTs between two heavy primary states, between two thermal states, and between a heavy primary state and a thermal state. When the two states differ in their classical, order-$c$ data, the distances are of order $c$, and the states are distinguishable already at the level of classical gravity; when the leading data coincide, the distances are of order $1/c$ at every order of the short interval expansion, so that the distinguishability becomes a perturbative quantum gravity effect. For a heavy primary state and its thermal counterpart, the leading contribution to the BD appears at order $\ell^8$ and is of order $c^0$, whereas the RBD is generically of order $c$, in line with the earlier finding that a heavy primary state and a thermal state share the same order-$c$ entanglement entropy but have different order-$c$ Rényi entropies in the short interval expansion.

titles.title: Subsystem quantum Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance in 2D CFTs and its holographic applications

abstracts.value:
We present a particle-level study of photon-induced production in Herwig~7, focusing on coherent, single-dissociative, and double-dissociative proton configurations. The simulation combines the Budnev elastic photon flux with an inelastic photon PDF, using the internal Herwig~7 matrix elements for $\gamma\gamma \to \ell^+\ell^-$ and $\gamma\gamma \to W^+W^- \to \ell^+\ell^-\nu\bar{\nu}$ as the central setup. Using a dedicated Rivet analysis, we compare hard-system kinematics, charged-particle activity, rapidity-gap observables, and distributions sensitive to forward proton remnants.

We find that variations in shower settings generally have modest effects on hard-system distributions in well-populated phase-space regions, whereas coherent and dissociative samples exhibit more pronounced differences in additional charged-particle activity and rapidity-gap observables. These results provide a useful baseline for modelling semi-exclusive photon-induced measurements at the LHC and identify observables that are particularly sensitive to dissociative activity in future Monte Carlo generator comparisons.

titles.title: Coherent and Dissociative Photon-Induced Production in Herwig 7

abstracts.value: This chapter provides a pedagogical and comprehensive introduction to parton fragmentation functions (FFs), the essential non-perturbative quantities in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) that describe the universal process of hadronization, the transition of quarks and gluons into observable hadrons. Formally defined as gauge-invariant matrix elements, the determination of FFs is achieved through global QCD analyses that synthesize world data from three primary processes: electron-positron annihilation, semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, and proton-proton collisions. This chapter covers the theoretical foundations of FFs, including their operator definitions and properties, the experimental probes used to constrain them, and the methodologies of modern global analyses. The discussion is extended to more advanced topics, including dihadron FFs, the three-dimensional picture of hadronization provided by spin- and transverse-momentum-dependent FFs, and the modification of fragmentation in a nuclear medium, which is key to probe their fundamental properties.

titles.title: Parton Fragmentation Functions

abstracts.value: The quantum phase of a multiparticle system has remained a long-standing mystery in quantum physics. The absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this physical quantity has prevented the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number. Here, we resolve this problem by measuring, for the first time, the quantum phase of multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles. We achieve this through a new quantum state tomography scheme that combines homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection. This approach enables us to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations and establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation. Our measurements further provide access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system, a fundamental resource for multiparticle quantum information processing. Furthermore, we report the spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase. These results provide an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.

titles.title: Measuring the Quantum Phase of Multiphoton Systems

abstracts.value: The use of entanglement in sensing is often motivated by improved sensitivity arising from non-classical correlations among probes. For static signals, however, this quantum advantage in Ramsey spectroscopy with $N$ probes is known to be highly susceptible to dephasing, which severely limits the possible gain from entanglement. In contrast, we consider sensing of signals that vary in time. Considering the simplest example of dephasing by classical white noise, we show that entanglement allows a large increase in bandwidth when estimating the frequency components of a time-dependent signal. Without sacrificing any sensitivity, entanglement allows for an increase in bandwidth by a factor of $N$. Alternatively, when interrogation times are limited by the signal bandwidth rather than by dephasing, the average estimation uncertainty over a fixed bandwidth is reduced by a factor of $\sqrt{N}$ compared with separable states.

titles.title: Entanglement-enhanced Ramsey spectroscopy of broadband signals

abstracts.value: The long-range Ising model is the prototype of criticality with power-law interactions. In each dimension its interacting critical points form a one-parameter family of nonlocal conformal field theories, weakly coupled at both ends but not in between. We study this family in one, two and three dimensions from several independent directions. We extend the expansion about the generalized free field from three to eight loops and expand about the short-range end. We show that Hamiltonian truncation applies to this nonlocal theory once a truncation artifact is corrected. Where they can be compared, the resummed expansions, Hamiltonian truncation, the numerical renormalization group and Monte Carlo simulations agree on the dimension of the leading $\mathbb{Z}_2$-even scalar at the sub-percent level, as universality requires.

titles.title: The long-range Ising CFT: perturbative and nonperturbative approaches

abstracts.value: Many quantum-information tasks can benefit from Gaussian quantum resources, while their fundamental performance limits are characterized by quantum information quantities. However, a unified perturbation theory for these quantities directly within the Gaussian-state formalism has been lacking. We develop such a theory for the von Neumann entropy, quantum relative entropy, quantum Chernoff quantity, and quantum fidelity, using perturbations of the moments of a reference Gaussian state. Using general Fréchet-derivative identities, we derive compact second-order expressions for reference-state covariance matrices whose symplectic eigenvalues are all greater than $1/2$. We also show that the perturbative quantum Chernoff quantity is maximized at its symmetric point, yielding the quantum Chernoff exponent (QCE). We further show that symplectic eigenvalues equal to 1/2 can lead to slower asymptotic vanishing, potentially improving the corresponding fundamental performance limits. For reference-state covariance matrices containing symplectic eigenvalues both equal to and greater than 1/2, we identify sufficient conditions under which the former determine the leading covariance-matrix contributions, allowing the remaining modes to be traced out without changing the leading-order asymptotic scaling or the coefficient. Applying the framework to quantum illumination and incoherent-light sub-Rayleigh object discrimination, we recover known asymptotic QCEs directly within the Gaussian-state formalism. In the latter problem, the slower asymptotic vanishing explains the known quadratic scaling of the QCE with the source separation.

titles.title: Perturbation theory for quantum information quantities of Gaussian states

abstracts.value: We use the Cross-Tracer Clustering Ratio (CTCR) acoustic response estimator, a new probe of morphology-dependent galaxy clustering in photometric surveys. CTCR is the ratio of the auto-power spectrum of early-type galaxies (ETGs) to their cross-power spectrum with late-type galaxies (LTGs). In the matched-kernel deterministic linear-bias limit the CTCR cancels the complete projected matter spectrum, including the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) wiggles, leaving only the relative linear bias. This makes the ratio uniquely sensitive to physics beyond deterministic linear bias: any residual acoustic structure in the CTCR must arise from a difference between the normalised non-linear responses of the two tracers. We, for the first time, exploit this property to model the measured ratio as a smooth scale-dependent baseline multiplied by a scale-dependent acoustic template, and constrain the amplitude $A_{\rm morph}$ of the differential acoustic response jointly with the BAO dilation parameter $α$. Applying the estimator to nine bins of the DESI Legacy Survey Data Release 8 spanning $0.1 < z < 0.9$, we obtain$α= 0.9997 \pm 0.0383$, consistent with the Planck 2018 $Λ$CDM prediction, and $A_{\rm morph} = 0.369 \pm 0.307$, consistent with zero. A Bayesian model comparison yields at most a 2.6$σ$ preference for the acoustic template over a smooth-only baseline. The estimator is model-independent, requires no external calibration of the absolute bias, and is directly applicable to the wide-field imaging surveys that will define the next decade of cosmology. It offers a new route to testing halo occupation and assembly-bias models, and an independent, systematics-robust cross-check of BAO measurements from spectroscopic surveys.

titles.title: A Morphology-Based Cross-Tracer Ratio for Robust BAO Tests

abstracts.value: Gravitational-wave dark sirens can be combined with galaxy catalogues to provide a measurement of the Hubble constant. This inference requires assigning each potential host galaxy a probability of hosting a merger, but the appropriate weighting is uncertain because the binary merger rate may trace different galaxy properties, such as stellar mass or star formation rate, depending on the underlying formation channel. We introduce a flexible framework in which the dark-siren population is described as a mixture of two host-weighting prescriptions, with the mixing fraction inferred jointly with $H_0$. These components may be interpreted as subpopulations associated with distinct binary-formation environments. Using simulated catalogues, we show that marginalising over uncertainty in the host-population mixture preserves unbiased constraints on $H_0$, while allowing the gravitational-wave data to constrain the relative contribution of the two host populations. In particular, an A#-like detector network with $\mathcal{O}(10^3)$ dark sirens may be able to exclude scenarios in which the host population traces only one of the two weighting prescriptions. Dark-siren analyses may therefore provide robust cosmological measurements and new information about how merging compact binaries trace the galaxy population.

titles.title: Hostbusters: constraining $H_0$ and binary formation channels through gravitational-wave host galaxy associations

abstracts.value: Consider several cavity resonators whose resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields are known, and suppose that they are coupled through apertures. How can the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of the resulting coupled-cavity resonator be expressed in terms of the original resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields? This is a problem frequently encountered in radio-frequency systems for accelerators. One example is a multicell cavity used in high-energy electron accelerators. In this note, the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of such coupled cavities are examined as generally as possible, based only on Maxwell's equations and boundary conditions. Specifically, the response function of a cavity as viewed from its coupling ports, namely, its admittance matrix, is derived, and a formulation is developed to express the coupled resonant electromagnetic fields using this matrix. The resulting formulation shows that the coupled resonant modes can be described in terms of overlap integrals between the resonant modes of the cavities and the waveguide modes at the coupling apertures. It also shows that the coupled resonant frequencies are given by the zeros of the determinant of a matrix constructed from the admittance matrices. The results thus obtained are applied to simple systems to confirm the validity of the formulation. Numerical calculations based on this formulation are also carried out for periodic systems in an attempt to derive dispersion relations.

titles.title: A General Treatment of Coupled Cavity Resonators

abstracts.value: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide a calibration-free measure of distances, offering important input on the long-standing tension between early- and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant ($H_0$). In the absence of an electromagnetic counterpart, the dark siren method can be employed to statistically correlate a gravitational wave event's localization with a galaxy catalog of potential hosts. We present a measurement of the Hubble constant using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey Data Release 3 and the fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog. Applying the dark siren method to a large, photometrically heterogeneous footprint required revised catalog-construction choices: a faint apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r<20$) to control known photometric-redshift bias, a bright apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r>15.5$) to exclude saturated sources, implementation of an evolving luminosity function parameterization, and de-biasing survey regions based on survey depth and photometric redshift precision. With these choices applied to DELVE, we obtain $H_0= 67.4^{+13.0}_{-11.2}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ from dark sirens alone, and $H_0= 70.6^{+8.7}_{-7.0}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ when combined with the bright siren GW170817. We test other galaxy catalog configuration choices, and find subdominant influence from photometric band choice and luminosity function parameterization on the final $H_0$ posterior. Our results demonstrate that extending the dark siren method to wider-area, non-uniform galaxy surveys is feasible and provides additional constraining power on $H_0$ relative to the spectral siren method, opening the door for analyses with forthcoming galaxy catalogs from LSST, Euclid, and Roman.

titles.title: Constraints on the Cosmic Expansion Rate Using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey and the Fifth Gravitational Wave Transient Catalog

abstracts.value: A $I^π$ = (29/2$^{+}$) metastable state with $T_{1/2}$$ > $ 10 s at $E_{x}$ = 2102 keV has been identified in the stable nucleus, $^{197}$Au. Such a decay pattern has not previously been identified in a long-lived nuclear state and serves as a sensitive probe of the interplay between shell structure, configuration mixing, and collective degrees of freedom. abstracts.value: Plasma simulations for magnetic-confinement fusion (MCF) involve high-dimensional kinetic dynamics, strong nonlinear coupling, complex geometries, and multiscale spatiotemporal behavior, imposing severe computational bottlenecks. While quantum computing offers a potential alternative for accelerating plasma simulation problems, its practical advantage for fusion research has not yet been demonstrated. We review existing quantum computing studies across kinetic dynamics, wave interactions, equilibrium, and macroscopic stability, evaluating their hardware implementations and operational bottlenecks. Current studies remain largely restricted to linearized equations, reduced models, or isolated computational subroutines, leaving a substantial gap from realistic fusion simulations. We summarize key problem characteristics, including high dimensionality, structured dynamics, and measurement requirements, under which plasma applications are most likely to yield a quantum advantage. Guided by these considerations, we highlight potential approaches and present a roadmap toward practical quantum advantage of simulating plasma in MCF.

titles.title: Quantum computing for plasma physics in magnetic-confinement fusion

abstracts.value: Quantum states are ultimately responsible for numerous counterintuitive phenomena that defy classical intuition. As the development of quantum technologies accelerates, our ability to harness these quantum resources becomes essential. This review addresses a fundamental question. How do we quantify the quantumness of a state, and which specific traits distinguish it from its classical counterparts? We examine quantumness through both theoretical and operational lenses, providing a clear framework for state characterization. Ultimately, we demonstrate that certifying quantumness is not just a theoretical exercise. It is a practical necessity for identifying, and realizing quantum advantage in real-world applications.

titles.title: How Quantum Is Light? Concepts, Measures, and Applications of Optical Quantumness

abstracts.value: We present late-time photometry (~100-400 days after peak) and nebular-phase optical/NIR spectroscopy (100-360 days) of the Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) SN 2023bee. This SN Ia was observed TESS immediately before and after explosion and showed a relatively weak early excess light-curve feature detected in multiple UV and optical bands. Possible explanations for this early excess feature include interaction between the SN ejecta and a non-degenerate companion, or the decay of radioactive isotopes synthesized near the ejecta surface in a sub-$\text{M}_\text{Ch}$ double-detonation scenario. However, the degeneracies and incompleteness of existing models have so far prevented a definitive conclusion about its progenitor system. Nebular-phase spectra provide a complementary probe of SN Ia progenitors by constraining stripped H/He-rich material and iron-group abundances sensitive to the progenitor white dwarf density. We report the non-detection of narrow H/He features in nebular phase optical/NIR spectra of SN 2023bee, placing upper limits of $m^{\text{stripped}}_\text{H}\lesssim5.0\times10^{-3}\text{ M}_\odot$ and $m_\text{He}^{\text{stripped}}\lesssim1.2\times10^{-4}\text{ M}_\odot$. These limits strongly disfavor a non-degenerate companion and suggest that companion interaction is unlikely to explain the early excess of SN 2023bee. We also performed line-diagnostic measurements on the 7200 Åcomplex using multi-Gaussian fitting and continuum estimation, with the inferred velocities validated against NIR spectrum at the similar phase. The resulting low Ni-to-Fe mass ratio, $m_\text{Ni}/m_\text{Fe}\lesssim 0.06$, is broadly consistent with a sub-$M_{\text{Ch}}$ double-detonation progenitor system.

titles.title: Constraints on the Progenitor of SN 2023bee from its Nebular-Phase Spectra

abstracts.value: In this work, we perform self-consistent isospin-invariant Skyrme density functional calculations to investigate the ground-state properties of the isospin triplets with mass numbers $A=70$, $74$, and $78$. abstracts.value: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) Collaboration recently reported a candidate event consistent with a high-energy nuclear recoil, motivating a possible interpretation by Lee, Takahashi, and Tsai involving the production of an invisible baryon-number-two scalar with a mass near $1.85$ GeV. Motivated by this hypothetical scenario, we investigate the $J^P=0^+$$uuddss$ hexaquark system using QCD sum rules. We consider five local diquark-diquark-diquark interpolating currents with different scalar and axial-vector diquark combinations, together with a baryon-baryon current constructed from two $Λ$-type baryon currents. The operator product expansions are calculated up to dimension sixteen, and their numerical behaviors are examined under different OPE truncations. Among the currents considered, only the $SU(3)_{\rm flavor}$-singlet current $J_{SSS}$, consisting of three scalar color-$\bar{\mathbf{3}}_C$ diquarks, yields a low-mass solution at $D=12$, with $M_{SSS}=1.85^{+0.19}_{-0.20}$ GeV. Interestingly, scalar color-$\bar{\mathbf{3}}_C$ diquarks belong to the flavor $\bar{\mathbf{3}}_F$ representation, and their local color-singlet construction has a unique nonvanishing flavor structure, $[ud][ds][su]$, corresponding to $uuddss$. Analogous all-scalar-diquark currents vanish for other flavor configurations, such as $uuuddd$ and $uuudds$. Together with our QCD sum-rule results, this property highlights the special role of the all-scalar-diquark configuration, $[ud][ds][su]$, as a possible deeply bound structure.
