abstracts.value: Radio interferometry relies on reconstruction techniques to form images from discrete visibility measurements. As instruments encompass wider fields of view, the nuance of that reconstruction can lead to geometrical errors in the image. As a result, the estimation of the flux density of sources can change. We derive the full functional analysis of widefield radio interferometry to provide a foundation for investigating geometry-based errors. We use this framework to investigate three examples: 1) deconvolution errors resulting from a minor iteration, 2) gridding errors resulting from excluding primary beam sidelobes, and 3) w-term errors resulting from omitting the non-coplanar dimension on a 2 min near-zenith transit. We use their adjoint operator descriptions to simulate each of the three cases for two fields using the Murchison Widefield Array. While the estimated errors on the flux density of reconstructed sources are small, overall errors depend on the field observed. For our two fields, we find fractional flux density errors up to 5% due to deconvolution, 0.1% due to gridding, and 10% due to non-coplanarity. Our operator formalism can be used to investigate many other forms of image reconstruction errors.

titles.title: Functional Analysis of Widefield Radio Interferometry

abstracts.value: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) has resolved horizon-scale emission in M87* and Sgr A*. Extending these observations to fainter black holes, multiple frequencies, and evolving structures requires greater sensitivity and new observing capabilities. We investigate how ALMA2040 could expand the scientific reach of global millimeter very long baseline interferometry (mm-VLBI), compared with ALMA's Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade (WSU). Phasing a larger ALMA array and enabling simultaneous observations across multiple ALMA bands would improve sensitivity and frequency phase transfer, providing spectral and polarimetric diagnostics of gravity, accretion flows, magnetic fields, and relativistic jets. In the configurations studied, ALMA2040 achieves sub-mJy baseline sensitivity at 230 GHz and improves prospects for faint-source imaging at 345 GHz, opening a path from individual horizon-scale targets toward population studies. Simulated observations of M87* show improved multi-frequency recovery of emission from the compact ring-like region toward the jet base, enabling studies of the accretion-jet connection. For Sgr A*, simulations of interstellar scattering mitigation yield a 27% reduction in the error of the recovered intrinsic source structure relative to the WSU configuration. Beyond black holes, these capabilities benefit geometric-distance measurements, stellar masers, compact transients, and other applications of high-resolution astrophysics. Together with rapid-response capabilities across the VLBI network, ALMA2040 could support a transition from isolated snapshots toward multi-frequency, time-resolved studies of compact sources.

titles.title: The transformative power of ALMA2040 for mm-VLBI

abstracts.value: The analysis of Hamiltonian Variational Ansätze centers on three fundamental questions: which states are exactly reachable from a given initial state, what native control depth suffices for local and global synthesis, and whether a bounded circuit extension can expose a direction of decreasing cost at a suboptimal output. We address these challenges by leveraging the dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) associated with the circuits and the geometry of the initial state's orbit under the action of the corresponding dynamical Lie group $G$. We show that an initial state has a closed projective orbit whenever it is a nondegenerate eigenstate of a control Hamiltonian. Combined with asymptotic QAOA convergence, this guarantees exact, finite depth ground state preparation for architectures employing diagonal problem Hamiltonians and irreducible stoquastic mixers. We bound the number of native control exponentials required for local unitary synthesis and state preparation using DLA commutator filtration growth alongside reachable orbit dimensions. Complementing these local results, we construct global frameworks on invariant sectors equipped with full unitary or special unitary dynamical Lie algebras. These constructions yield explicit applications to Pauli-generated systems and constrained maximum independent set multi-angle QAOA circuits; specifically, we show that their native control costs are directly determined by commutator filtration depth and independent-set toggle-group geometry, respectively. Finally, if the dynamical Lie group is compact, the observable $H_P$ generates an admissible evolution ($iH_P \in \mathfrak{g}$, where $\mathfrak{g}$ is the DLA), and the projective orbit of the initial state contains a ground state ray of $H_P$, then a bounded depth, identity-initialized circuit extension exhibits either first-order descent or negative curvature at every suboptimal circuit output.

titles.title: Circuit Synthesis for Variational Quantum Algorithms: The Depth of Algebra and Geometry

abstracts.value: Here we demonstrate a new AI/ML based image reconstruction method for coded-aperture instruments that provides a pathway for embedded real-time use on-board spaceflight missions. Using the Swift Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) for our initial simulated demonstration, we used our new technique to replace the standard Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) based image reconstruction pipeline. In our alternative approach, we have created a neural network that maps detector counts directly to source positions using simulated responses from selected Swift Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) observations. The network combines convolutional feature extraction with attention and is trained at around 900 source counts. Under zero background noise, it achieves over 93% exact-pixel localization accuracy with 400 detected source photons. The model maintains at least 90% exact-pixel localization accuracy with up to 8,500 added background counts for sources with 900 detected photons. Within the evaluated region of BAT's field of view, these results show that source position can be recovered from sparse coded-aperture measurements in a wide-field instrument. A key feature of this technique is that explicit inclusion of the mask pattern is not required. This allows us to train the algorithm to "see" using data accumulated from an imaging system. These new non-traditional imaging techniques show substantial promise in enabling efficient imaging using non-planar geometries, which will enable new classes of hard X/$γ$-ray imaging systems and simultaneously improve imaging capability for currently operating instruments.

titles.title: A New AI/ML Based Image Reconstruction Technique for Hard X-ray Coded Aperture Imagers

abstracts.value: Precise measurements of single top-quark production in the associated $tW$-channel require efficient discrimination against the dominant $t\bar{t}$ background. In this work, we investigate the applicability of quantum machine learning to this classification problem using the Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) algorithm. Simulated proton-proton collision events from CMS Open Data corresponding to Run-2 are employed to train and evaluate the VQC model. Its performance is compared with two established classical approaches, Boosted Decision Trees (BDTs) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) using both machine learning metrics and physics-motivated metrics that describe the Signal Significance as a function of Signal Efficiency. The comparison is performed separately for the dileptonic $e-μ$ channel and for the resolved and boosted hadronic topologies. In addition, signal-enriched and background-enriched phase-space regions are studied to assess the dependence of classifier performance on event topology. Our results provide a systematic benchmark for the application of VQC for a realistic High Energy Physics classification task and identify the analysis regimes wherein quantum-inspired models offer competitive discrimination with respect to established classical techniques.

titles.title: A comparative study of variational quantum classifiers and classical machine learning for $tW-t\bar{t}$ discrimination at the LHC

abstracts.value: We consider quantum A-periods of local ${\mathbb P}^1 \times {\mathbb P}^1$, or equivalently the generating function of constant terms for powers of the Laurent polynomial $x + x^{-1} + y + y^{-1}$ where $x$ and $y$ are $q$-commuting variables. We derive a number of new representations for these rich combinatorial and algebraic objects. First, we find that the well-known TBA equation encodes not only the A-period itself but also higher diagonal modes of the corresponding noncommutative Laurent polynomials. Second, we obtain new formulas for the period in terms of continued fractions and related orthogonal polynomials, as well as a nontrivial explicit recursion allowing its efficient computation. Finally, we compute quantum corrections to the classical Picard-Fuchs equation, and observe that holonomicity of the classical period does not generalise to $q$-holonomicity of its quantum counterpart. Applications to random walks on the Cayley graph of the Heisenberg group, and related new approaches to more efficient generative AI systems, are outlined.

titles.title: Quantum Periods from TBA and Continued Fractions

abstracts.value: Here we report atomic structure calculations and experimental observations of the two-photon $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition in Yb. The unique level structure of Yb places the $6s6p\;^1P_1$ state's energy at $\approx\!49.7\%$ of the ionization energy, which facilitates two-photon Doppler-free excitation of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state from the $6s^2\;^1S_0$ ground state at a relatively low optical intensity. This $J= 0 \rightarrow J=0$ transition is immune to first-order Zeeman and electric quadrupole shifts, has reduced sensitivity to higher-order Zeeman shifts, and is further predicted to have relatively low sensitivity to density shifts. Using configuration interaction theory, we compute relevant properties of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state for sensing, including the $C_6$ coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, and BBR depopulation rate. As a first experimental step, we demonstrate two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition. From our experimental spectra, we estimate the natural linewidth (lifetime) of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ state to be 90 kHz (1.8 $μ$s). We believe this transition, or other $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6sns\;^1S_0$ transitions in Yb with $n\approx23$, may find use in a variety of sensing applications, potentially including a two-photon clock, electrometer, or BBR thermometer.

titles.title: Two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg transition for quantum sensing in ytterbium

abstracts.value: To investigate low-energy incomplete fusion (ICF) dynamics, the excitation functions (EFs) of different evaporation residues (ERs) produced in <math><mrow><mrow/><mmultiscripts><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>12</mn></mmultiscripts><mo>+</mo><mrow/><mmultiscripts><mi>Te</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>130</mn></mmultiscripts></mrow></math> system were measured in the 4–7 MeV/nucleon energy range using the recoil-catcher activation technique followed by off-line <math><mi>γ</mi></math>-ray spectroscopy and analyzed in the framework of statistical model code pace4. It has been found that cross sections for <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> channels were well reproduced by the code, suggesting that they originate from complete fusion (CF) reactions. In contrast, the <math><mi>α</mi></math>-emitting channels display a marked enhancement over theoretical predictions, pointing to the contribution of incomplete fusion (ICF) processes arising from projectile breakup. abstracts.value: Electron cloud effects constitute a major performance limitation in high-intensity particle accelerators such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). A key ingredient for understanding and modeling these effects is the energy distribution of electrons impinging on the vacuum chamber walls. In this paper, we present direct measurements of electron cloud energy distributions obtained in the LHC Vacuum Pilot Sector (VPS) using retarding field analyzers with a beam pipe diameter of 8 cm, i.e., twice the LHC arc one. The VPS provides a dedicated, fully instrumented test environment for electron cloud studies under real LHC beam conditions. The measured energy spectra systematically exhibit a low-energy component associated with secondary electron emission and a higher-energy component originating from bunch-driven acceleration. To characterize these features, a phenomenological model is developed to reproduce the observed distributions up to 3 keV. Model parameters are extracted from a large dataset of LHC fills, with a representative 2025 physics fill used for detailed illustration. The evolution of the accelerated-electron peak is analyzed throughout the fill cycle and compared with predictions from the analytical kick approximation model. Good agreement is observed—particularly during the stable beam phase in one beamline—confirming that bunch-induced kicks dominate the electron energy gain in the field-free regions, as for the VPS. Discontinuities in the peak energy at operational transitions, as well as the recurrent observation of narrow accelerated peaks in the other beamline, are reported and suggest a dependence of the beam optics on the resulting energy gain. Finally, cumulative energy distribution functions are derived to quantify the fraction of electrons exceeding given energy thresholds. These results establish a quantitative experimental reference for energy-resolved electron cloud modeling in the LHC, providing direct inputs for electron cloud simulation benchmarking, heat load estimates, ESD modeling, and residual electron background assessment in ion diagnostics.

titles.title: Electron cloud energy distribution measurement and model in the LHC with the Vacuum Pilot Sector

abstracts.value: Recent experiments in circuit quantum acoustodynamics (cQAD) have demonstrated on-chip multimode phononic interactions and single-mode phonon squeezing [von Lüpke , Nat. Phys. 20, 564 (2024)], yet the generation of bistable squeezing and the redistribution of squeezing across multiple mechanical modes remain largely unexplored. Here we propose a scheme to generate and controllably redistribute bistable phonon squeezing in a cQAD system consisting of a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to two high-overtone bulk acoustic resonator modes. By exploiting the intrinsic Kerr nonlinearity of the qubit under a single-tone microwave drive, we uncover a robust bistability in the steady states of both the qubit and the two phonon modes. We systematically map out distinct stability regimes and show that, within the bistable region, the degree and orientation of squeezing become branch-dependent—a direct manifestation of bistable quantum fluctuations. Remarkably, both the qubit and the second phonon mode can surpass the standard quantum limit, achieving up to 3 dB of steady-state squeezing with experimentally accessible parameters. Moreover, by tuning the mode detunings, the squeezing resources of the qubit can be efficiently redistributed to the two phonon modes, enabling targeted control over phononic squeezing. Our proposal is fully compatible with current cQAD platforms and provides a practical route toward engineering nonclassical states of motion for quantum information processing and sensing, where bistable squeezing offers an additional degree of freedom for noise suppression and quantum-state switching.

titles.title: Bistable squeezing in a multimode circuit-quantum-acoustodynamics system

abstracts.value: Probabilistic photon sources (PPSs) are the most mature quantum light sources and offer a practical route toward a quantum-repeater-based quantum internet. However, the intrinsic noise from multiphoton emission has hindered the construction of global-scale quantum repeaters with multiple elementary links. Recently, the multiplexed quantum repeater protocol based on time measurements (MQR-TM) combined high heralding rates with phase robustness in entanglement generation, making it compatible with both fiber and free-space quantum channels. Nevertheless, scaling MQR-TM to multiple links remains challenging because intrinsic multiphoton noise compromises the faithful swapping and further distribution of temporal entanglement. Here, we develop an efficient time-to-polarization conversion method and incorporate polarization-encoded entanglement swapping into MQR-TM, which filters intrinsic noise while preserving the efficient and phase-robust temporal entanglement generation. Furthermore, by using free-space backbone channels to minimize the nesting level, we show that this MQR-TM-based architecture attains a subhertz entanglement distribution rate over 10 000 km with a fidelity exceeding 90%, using feasible parameters for quantum memories and PPSs.

titles.title: Reliable global entanglement distribution based on probabilistic photon sources

abstracts.value: We investigate photon motion, black-hole shadows, weak gravitational lensing, and image magnification for a charged static black hole in bumblebee gravity immersed in dispersive plasma environments. The bumblebee field introduces spontaneous Lorentz-symmetry breaking through the dimensionless parameter <math altimg="si97.svg" display="inline" id="d1e1567"><mi>L</mi></math>, while the electric charge is characterized by <math altimg="si99.svg" display="inline" id="d1e1572"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>. Photon propagation is treated with the Hamiltonian formalism for a cold non-magnetized plasma. A homogeneous plasma and a non-uniform power-law profile are used in the photon-sphere and shadow analyses, while homogeneous and singular-isothermal-sphere (SIS) plasmas are considered in the weak-lensing analysis We first determine the allowed black-hole domain from the horizon condition and then compute the photon-sphere radius, optical shadow radius, EHT-compatible angular shadow size, weak deflection angle, and magnification observables. The results show that increasing the charge-to-mass ratio decreases the photon-sphere and shadow radii and suppresses the weak deflection angle, while the Lorentz-violating parameter produces a milder but systematic reduction of these observables through its coupling to the charge sector. Plasma dispersion shifts the photon sphere outward but reduces the apparent shadow radius; in contrast, its effect on weak lensing depends on the plasma profile, enhancing the homogeneous-plasma deflection while slightly suppressing the SIS-plasma deflection. We further confront the theoretical shadow with the Event Horizon Telescope measurements of M87* and Sgr A*. The EHT angular diameters, <math altimg="si3.svg" display="inline" id="d1e1582"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M87∗</mi></mrow></msub><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mo><mn>42</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>3</mn><mspace class="nbsp" width="0.33em"/><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">as</mi></mrow></math> and <math altimg="si4.svg" display="inline" id="d1e1607"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Sgr A∗</mi></mrow></msub><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mo><mn>48.7</mn><mo>±</mo><mn>7</mn><mspace class="nbsp" width="0.33em"/><mi>μ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">as</mi></mrow></math>, translate into exclusion regions in the <math altimg="si49.svg" display="inline" id="d1e1631"><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> parameter space and show that charge, Lorentz violation, and plasma dispersion are strongly degenerate in shadow-based tests. These results demonstrate that simultaneous use of shadow constraints, weak deflection, and magnification can provide complementary probes of Lorentz-violating charged black-hole spacetimes in realistic plasma environments.

abstracts.value: Classical causal set theory models spacetime causality by locally finite partial orders. Because partial orders are antisymmetric, they cannot represent distinct elements that are mutually causally related, as would occur in a discrete analog of a chronology-violating region. We develop a locally finite discrete framework that allows closed causal loops and yields a locally finite partial order upon identifying mutually related elements. Each class of mutually related elements is collapsed to one point in the induced poset, and its cardinality is assigned as a finite weight to the corresponding point. Within this setting we define maximum causal time using simple finite paths and prove an equidistance characterization: members of one chronology-violating class have the same discrete proper-time distance from any event in their common past or future, with a finite correction for the closed path inside the class. We also study the special case in which the relation is generated by iterating a single self-map <math display="inline"><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>X</mi></math>; cycles of <math display="inline"><mi>f</mi></math> then give explicit finite closed causal loops. Finally, we define two finite counting invariants: the proportion of elements in chronology-violating classes and the normalized mean of <math display="inline"><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. We study the mathematical properties of these discrete causal structures; no equations of motion or probabilities for their occurrence are specified. The construction does not assert a continuum-discrete correspondence in the chronology-violating case, and ordinary causets are recovered when all equivalence classes are singletons.

titles.title: Chronology violation on locally finite quasiordered sets

abstracts.value: Galaxy-galaxy lensing (GGL) measurements around galaxy samples in different environments provide valuable information about the galaxy-halo connection. In such studies the halo model is commonly used to estimate physical parameters from the lensing signal, but the impact of environment is generally not considered. Our aim is to adapt the halo model to allow a density-split GGL analysis and to understand the environmental dependence of the elements of the model. We use the FLAMINGO suite of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations to construct samples of halos in underdense and overdense regions. Environment density is assigned to halos based on halo counts within an aperture, employing different aperture sizes to probe both local and large scales. We utilize spherical apertures with radii between $1 h^{-1} {\rm Mpc}$ and $10 h^{-1} {\rm Mpc}$. We find a strong dependence on environment for the halo mass function (HMF) and the halo bias. To account for this, we propose an empirical modification that can be applied to existing HMF prescriptions. We find that after a density split, the halo bias is approximately constant with mass. There is also an environmental dependence for the stellar-to-halo-mass relation (SHMR), the conditional stellar mass function, and the mass-concentration relation, all of which can be addressed with existing models. We evaluate the impact of overlooking environment on halo occupation distribution (HOD) parameter inference, finding that it leads to biased estimations of the SHMR and the satellite fraction. These results emphasize the need to review the assumptions adopted in the halo model when working with samples of galaxies binned by environment, and consequently, by galaxy properties that correlate with environment, such as morphology and color.

titles.title: Environmental dependence in the halo model informed by the FLAMINGO simulations

abstracts.value: Inflationary cosmology faces a fundamental gap between primordial quantum fluctuations and the classical cosmic history inferred from observations. Although the primordial quantum state is a superposition of field configurations, standard cosmology assumes one definite realization of curvature perturbations and uses classical perturbation theory to describe the resulting gravitational potentials, CMB anisotropies, and large-scale structure. Squeezing and decoherence of primordial fluctuations alone do not explain why this one-realization description is physically meaningful. We address this issue through Cosmological Classical Branches (CCBs), using the quantum-information-theoretic notion of physical records. In CCBs, distinct late-time matter components carry compatible records of the same primordial configuration. A record in one component makes that configuration readable, while a disjoint compatible record suppresses interference accessible to operations on the first. Each branch thus admits a common c-number primordial label at finite resolution, while the global quantum superposition persists. This Letter summarizes the framework developed in Ref.~\cite{Kuroda2026CCB}.

titles.title: How do late-time photons "record" primordial curvature perturbations?

abstracts.value: We regularize the central density cusp of the Joshi--Malafarina--Narayan spacetime using a normalized kernel motivated by a zero-point length. For an unbounded cusp, the convolution and enclosed mass are obtained analytically; truncating this density gives a regular, horizonless tangential-pressure interior matched to Schwarzschild. Convolving the finite cloud instead preserves its total mass and yields a smooth matter tail. A compactness bound establishes horizon avoidance for this second prescription. We determine the central lapse, establish causal geodesic completeness despite extreme optical delays, derive a uniform optical-delay formula across the critical compactness, and identify the stable interior light ring of ultracompact configurations. The massless scalar probe operator is nonnegative, while semiclassical trapped modes exhibit strongly suppressed leakage. An explicit pressure-closure comparison separates robust geometric properties from closure-dependent delay exponents. Planck-scale examples illustrate extreme redshifts and delays, but their photon interpretation requires physics beyond classical propagation in the core. The construction specifies an effective static source, rather than a microscopic matter theory or a dynamical resolution of collapse.

titles.title: Dressing a naked singularity with zero-point length

abstracts.value: Optical neutrino telescopes reduce the photomultiplier signals of an optical module or string segment to compact multichannel summaries, and readout loss can make these summaries unreliable. We asked whether availability-based quality gates, which accept a summary when enough of the readout was live, can certify a summary of inter-channel statistical consistency (called coherence here; not optical coherence) under readout loss, and where they fail. We used public IceCube pulses (9,484 string records) and the released hits of KM3NeT event KM3-230213A with controlled readout loss, together with a replay of real KM3NeT readout flags. In a two-by-two design we compared a published recursive support state with direct mask support, and calibrated every threshold on development records. The support state is a function of the mask and added no information. On IceCube the support-gated rule retained 0.16 percentage points more usable summaries, an effect of the window at which support was read that reversed sign at a looser tolerance; on KM3NeT it accepted nothing. The gates accepted only records with nearly intact masks, including records whose charge had been depleted by signal-dependent loss that the mask does not record. Pulse loss during live acquisition and timing jitter passed every availability gate, which then accepted summaries of which up to 66% were unreliable. Availability flags are therefore necessary but not sufficient, and signal-based checks are needed. This work uses public data and is not an IceCube or KM3NeT Collaboration result.

titles.title: Missing Light, Misleading Confidence: Optical-Module Readout Loss and Signal Reliability in Neutrino Telescopes

abstracts.value: Implicit discretizations of transient heat conduction repeatedly generate sparse linear systems, making diffusion problems a natural test bed for quantum linear solvers. This study evaluates how accurately a variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) recovers the temperature field produced by one backward-Euler step of one-dimensional conduction on IBM quantum hardware. A pre-specified confirmatory experiment compares N=4 interior temperatures encoded on two qubits with N=8 temperatures encoded on three qubits using ten paired hardware blocks; a separately defined N=16, four-qubit extension is evaluated in five independently scheduled exploratory blocks. Local VQLS optimization reduces relative temperature-field error to approximately 10^{-8} for all three cases, establishing an essentially exact ideal reference at this scale. On hardware, mean relative L2 temperature-field error is 8.07% for N=4 and 20.14% for N=8, a paired increase of 12.06 percentage points (95% CI, 10.71-13.42; exact paired sign-flip p=0.001953). The exploratory N=16 mean is 24.75+/-1.84%. A pre-specified N=16 shot-count follow-up then evaluates the same locked circuit at 2,048, 8,192, and 32,768 shots in six independently scheduled blocks. Mean field error remains 23.64%, 24.57%, and 24.37%, respectively; the 32,768-minus-2,048-shot contrast is +0.74 percentage points (95% CI, -0.65 to 2.12; p=0.281). In contrast, ideal multinomial sampling predicts a reduction from 2.68% to 0.75%. Higher shot counts reduce block-to-block variability but do not recover the mean cold-side temperature field. The results show that full-field readout of a strongly nonuniform thermal state is limited by more than ordinary finite-shot sampling under the tested hardware conditions, motivating observable-focused quantum formulations for heat flux, stored energy, and selected temperatures.

titles.title: Transient Heat Conduction on Quantum Hardware: Replicated Temperature-Field Reconstruction and Shot-Count Sensitivity with a Variational Quantum Linear Solver

abstracts.value: The quest to understand the properties of matter at supranuclear densities found in the cores of neutron stars has intrigued physicists for a long time. The study addresses this problem using a physics-informed machine learning approach guided by astrophysical observations. The transformer model is trained on an agnostically generated ensemble of equations of state. Two geometric parameters are defined on the mass-radius sequence of a neutron star—the front bending and the back bending. The model provides a two-step solution: first, the model predicts the maximum mass and radius using the bending parameters, and then reconstructs the square of the sound-speed profile, completing the inverse mapping to the equation of state. Our results show that massive neutron stars are associated with sound-speed profiles that peak at relatively low densities, leading to strong back bending and a low-density stiff equation of state, indicating an early transition to quark matter and making the density at the core of massive stars comparatively less. The maximum mass for a neutron star predicted by the astrophysical constrained transformer model is 2.477 solar masses, and a minimum radius of about 11.498 km for a canonical mass of 1.4 solar masses.

titles.title: Physics-informed machine learning formulation to infer the inverse problem using the mass-radius geometry of neutron stars

abstracts.value: We investigate how local particle reservoirs can probe transport and density profiles in tilted spinless fermion chains with nearest-neighbor interactions. Using finite-chain Lindblad calculations with particle injection and extraction at opposite ends, we define a threshold-dependent transmission range from the stationary current as the chain length is varied. This range decreases with increasing tilt and follows the trends of the equilibrium density-crossover width in the parameter regimes studied. Interactions can enhance transmission by compensating field-induced energy costs, whereas strongly polarized configurations suppress transport. A third, weakly coupled extraction reservoir provides a complementary spatial probe: its current is exactly proportional to the local occupation in the presence of the probe, and the normalized current approaches the unperturbed nonequilibrium density as the probe coupling vanishes. We illustrate the detection of staggered density modulations and show that bulk densities can continue to relax after boundary currents have nearly stabilized. These protocols connect current measurements to spatial transmission and density structure in driven interacting chains.

titles.title: Probing nonequilibrium transport and density profiles in tilted interacting fermion chains with local reservoirs

abstracts.value: Black holes pose a lot of unsolved problems surrounding their fundamental properties. One of those puzzles is the black hole entropy problem. It has been known for a long time that black holes behave as thermodynamic systems and possess an entropy, but the question remains which microstates are responsible for this entropy. A theory of quantum gravity is needed to tackle this problem, currently the most viable example of which is string theory. The work of Strominger and Vafa, where they studied a class of asymptotically flat black holes, proves that string theory is indeed rich enough to account for the microstates responsible for the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Recently, the focus has shifted to asymptotically AdS black holes after the discovery of the AdS/CFT correspondence.Holographic dualities, the first example of which was discovered by Maldacena, have proven to be highly successful in providing a microstate counting for the entropy of black holes. The black hole is constructed on the gravity side of the correspondence, and the dual field theory counts its states. In this thesis we study black holes in AdS5 and their dual 4d N=1 SCFTs. The general procedure can be summarized as follows. On the field theory side, supersymmetric states are counted using the superconformal index. From the index we can obtain the entropy via a Legendre transform. By requiring that the entropy is real, we obtain a prediction for the existence of a dual black hole with that same entropy. In the dual supergravity theory we look for such solutions and compute the Euclidean on-shell action to match to the index, and the horizon area to match to the CFT entropy.This procedure was successfully applied to the minimal sector of any AdS5/CFT4 duality by Cabo-Bizet, Cassani, Martelli and Murthy, to leading order in the large N expansion. Here we aim to move beyond these results by adding flavour symmetries to the problem and by going beyond leading order at large N. On the field theory side of the duality, we study the index and entropy of flavoured SCFTs. We observe that for some theories, the simple procedure for taking the Legendre transform in the literature can no longer be applied. In all previously known examples, the index satisfies a cubic identity which leads to a simple way of deriving the entropy. We show that this identity no longer holds for certain theories but can be replaced by a sixth order identity, resulting in a different, more complicated expression for the entropy. These results suggest the existence of a new class of dual black hole solutions to match this entropy with their horizon area.We then proceed to finding these new solutions. This is a highly nontrivial problem because the dual supergravity theories contain hypermultiplet scalars. We specifically choose to work in the duality derived from M5-branes wrapping around a Riemann surface, between a family of non-Lagrangian class S SCFTs and a set of N=2 supergravities with two vector multiplets and one hypermultiplet, both parametrized by a rational number z. For z=±1, the cubic identity is satisfied and the entropy takes the familiar, simple form. Here we can easily identify the dual black holes through a relation to the five-dimensional STU model. For other values of z, we need the sixth order identity and we must include the hypermultiplet scalars in the black hole solution. To simplify the problem, we look for the near-horizon extremal geometry and restrict to two equal angular momenta. We start from the known solution for z=1 and perform an expansion around this point. We find an analytical solution to first order in the expansion. Since we only solve in the near-horizon region, we lose access to the on-shell action and chemical potentials but can still compute the charges and the entropy. The entropy through the area law matches precisely with the field theory prediction. We therefore prove that these partial solutions are the first step towards identifying the new class of black hole solutions with non-zero hypermultiplet scalars.In the final part of this thesis we move beyond the leading order at large N and add higher-derivative corrections. We focus on the universal case where only the R-symmetry is turned on. In this case, the higher-derivative action including four derivatives can be fully determined up to two constants, which can be related to the conformal anomalies of the dual field theory using the holographic map. We then set out to confirm the first subleading corrections to the index and entropy from the gravity side of the duality. We argue that the corrections to the black hole solution are not needed for the Euclidean on-shell action. It suffices to substitute the leading order solution in the corrected action. We perform this calculation carefully and obtain a precise match with the superconformal index. For the entropy, the corrections to the solution are needed. Here we opt to compute the entropy from the quantum statistical relation and the first law. Finally, we comment on higher-derivative corrections to flavoured theories.

abstracts.value: Direct Rydberg-Rydberg interactions decay rapidly with distance, limiting blockade-based gates between spatially separated neutral-atom qubits. We study a hybrid architecture in which a trapped ion mediates an additional effective interaction between two Rydberg atoms in optical tweezers. Following the ion-mediated mechanism [S. Mudli, S. Mal. S. S. Rej, A. Dey, and B. Deb, Phys. Rev. A 110, 062618 (2024)], we identify the total blockade interaction that enters the conditional gate dynamics and state the perturbative conditions under which the second-order Magnus description applies. We then use Floquet-modulated ground-Rydberg drives to construct cnot and controlled-\(T\) gates for a prescribed strong-blockade ratio. Numerical simulations show fidelities above 0.998 in the coherent model and reduced sensitivity to the sampled Rabi-frequency and detuning errors. Atomic spontaneous emission lowers the fidelity, with the shorter controlled-\(T\) sequence being less affected than the cnot sequence. We distinguish these effective-blockade simulations from a complete experimental error budget: ion heating, excess micromotion, trap-frequency noise, and residual atom-motion entanglement are not included numerically and must be controlled in an implementation. The results establish a concrete connection between ion-mediated blockade enhancement and Floquet-robust conditional control while defining the regime and limitations of the effective model.

abstracts.value: We consider scenarios in which a shallow bound state undergoes breakup by a probe whose energy is high compared to the binding energy. The first two scenarios, which serve as warm-up exercises, involve a single heavy particle bound to a light particle, analogous to a core nucleus bound to a neutron. We show that in quasifree kinematics, the leading effect comes from the heavy particle being knocked out by the probe, with corrections suppressed by inverse powers of the probe momentum. This formally justifies extracting neutron form factors from high-energy deuteron breakup in quasifree kinematics. In scenario 1, the probe is a local current; in scenario 2, it is hadron scattering. In scenarios 3 and 4 we consider, respectively, a local current and hadron scattering, but now on a three-body bound state of a heavy particle and two light particles. Hard knockout of the heavy particle leaves two low-energy particles behind, which can interact with one another. In all four scenarios, we prove that the amplitude is dominated by the nearby on-shell pole of the heavy-particle propagator and derive a closed-form expression for this contribution. When two bodies are left behind, the leading amplitude is the product of the scattering of the two light particles, a dynamical function depending on the probe, and a real function related to the bound-state wave function. Thus, quasifree removal of a core nucleus from a system with halo neutrons provides access to on-shell data on multineutron interactions. The resulting amplitudes are relativistic and satisfy unitarity for the remnant subsystem exactly. We also provide complementary nonrelativistic derivations. While the derivations are for spinless particles, the generalization to spin is straightforward, since the results depend only on quasifree knockout kinematics; we make no assumptions about the interparticle dynamics.

titles.title: Factorization in quasifree breakup reactions with two bodies left behind

abstracts.value: The Michelson interferometer underpins modern optical metrology, enabling precise measurements of displacement and gravitational waves. However, the sensitivity of the conventional Hermitian Michelson interferometer is inherently limited by its linear response to a perturbation. Here, we propose a non-Hermitian Michelson interferometer by introducing a coupling between two arms with reservoir engineering, forming a configuration of light cross. The eigenfrequency splitting as a spectral response displays a square-root dependence on a perturbation. Remarkably, the quantum Fisher information of our non-Hermitian Michelson interferometer can exceed that of its Hermitian counterpart by more than three orders when Brownian noise is included, implying a great enhancement in sensitivity. This work provides a framework for non-Hermitian interferometric sensing with unprecedented sensitivity.

titles.title: Non-Hermitian Michelson interferometer for exceptional-point-enhanced sensing

                  <jats:p>We investigate a coupled $\phi$CDM cosmological model in which energy exchange between dark energy and dark matter is governed by the derivative interaction term $Q = 3\alpha \dot{\rho}_m$. We constrain the model using baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from DESI Data Release~2, combined with compressed CMB likelihoods and  Type~Ia supernova datasets, including Pantheon$^{+}$, DES-Dovekie, and Union3. Parameter estimation is performed via Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, and Bayesian evidence is used for model comparison with $\Lambda$CDM. We find that the interaction parameter $\alpha$ is tightly constrained at the $\mathcal{O}(10^{-4})$ level and remains consistent with zero within $1\sigma$ across all dataset combinations, indicating no statistically significant evidence for dark sector interaction. The dark energy equation-of-state parameter remains close to $w_{\phi}=-1$, with only mild and statistically insignificant deviations toward a quintessence-like regime. While the inferred Hubble parameter shows a slight shift to higher values relative to $\Lambda$CDM, it remains insufficient to resolve the $H_0$ tension. The matter density parameter is consistent between both models within uncertainties. Bayesian model comparison consistently favors the $\Lambda$CDM model, with evidence ranging from moderate to strong depending on the dataset combination. Overall, the \textcolor{red}{coupled} $\phi$CDM model does not provide a significant improvement over the standard cosmological scenario in light of current observations.</jats:p>

titles.title: Cosmological Constraints and Bayesian Evidence for Coupled $\phi$CDM with DESI DR2 Observations

Models Developed to Describe FRIIb and

FRIIa Radio Sources

Ruth A. Daly a,1

aPresent address: Department of Physics, Penn State University, Tulpehocken

Road, P. O. Box 7009, Reading, PA 19610-6009

Abstract

Several models developed to describe the properties of FRIIa and FRIIb radio
sources are compared and contrasted here. The fundamental picture of a classical

double (edge-brightened, FRII) radio source powered by highly collimated outflows
from a central compact object is common to most models. However, models do differ

substantially, and some of the key differences are discussed here. Models must be
tested and constrained by comparisons with radio data. The extensive, detailed,
radio data that can be used to constrain the physical properties of FRII sources will

be described.

The radio bridge properties of FRII sources indicates they should be divided into
two categories: FRIIa and FRIIb sources. Low-power FRIIa sources are typically

found at low-redshift and have distorted radio bridge structure. High-power FRIIb
sources are typically found at high-redshift and have fairly regular, “cigar-like”

bridge shapes. It is anticipated that two model formalisms may be needed to describe
FRIIb and FRIIa sources. Unlike FRIIa sources, FRIIb sources are found to inhabit

gaseous environments similar to those found in low-redshift clusters of galaxies,
though the sources have redshifts between zero and two. Thus, FRIIb sources most

likely lie in clusters of galaxies. The importance of X-ray measurements to determine
the density and temperature of the gas in the vicinity of FRIIb sources is stressed.

1 Introduction

This is an exciting time for radio astronomy and the study of radio sources!
Our understanding of powerful, extended (FRII) radio sources has been sig-
nificantly developed through a combination of observational and theoretical
breakthroughs. Some of these will be presented and discussed here.

1 E-mail: rdaly@psu.edu

Preprint submitted to Elsevier Preprint 15 September 1999



The paper begins with a presentation of the general properties of models cur-
rently being used to describe FRII radio sources. All models require assump-
tions, and one of the basic differences between models is the assumptions that
are adopted before the model is applied; these differences will be discussed
in §2. Key observational aspects of the sources that must be addressed by
any model will be presented in §3. Given that a model is able to accurately
reproduce the observed characteristics of one or more sources, the application
of the model to large (possibly inhomogeneous) samples of sources will be
discussed. The statistical properties of very large samples MAY provide some
constraints, but ONLY after it has been shown that the model can accurately
reproduce the properties of one (and hopefully of many) individual sources in
detail.

It will be shown in §3 that the observed properties of FRII sources indicate
they should be divided into two distinct categories: FRIIa, and FRIIb sources.
The division should be based on radio bridge structure, but can also be based
on radio power, since the two are tightly coupled (Leahy & Williams 1984;
Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens 1989). Based on the different observational prop-
erties of each category, it is likely that a model that accurately describes FRIIa
sources will not accurately describe FRIIb sources, and vise versa. Thus, great
care should be taken in applying a model, especially if the application is to
a large sample of sources that contains both FRIIa and FRIIb sources. In
addition, care should be taken in applying a model to radio galaxies and ra-
dio loud quasars. This is especially true when the comparison is statistical, as
discussed in §3. The role of projection effects, and methods to determine the
projection angle of a source are presented in §4.

Source sizes and lifetimes are discussed in §5. Again, one can take the ap-
proach of studying individual sources in great detail, or considering statistical
properties of a very large sample. Of course, since there are likely to be two
distinct types of FRII sources, and since radio galaxies and radio loud quasars
have different statistical properties, the large sample would have to be ap-
propriately subdivided before any meaningful statistical properties could be
extracted. Much can be learned by studying individual sources in great detail.
If a particular model for source sizes and lifetimes can not explain the prop-
erties of a given source or a homogeneous class of sources, it seems premature
to apply the model to a very large sample of inhomogeneous sources.

Conclusions follow in §6.

2



2 General Properties of Models for FRII Radio Sources

2.1 What Most People Seem To Agree On

There are several aspects of models developed to describe FRII sources that
are common to most models, and that most researchers agree are likely to
be correct. First: almost everyone agrees that the original models of Scheuer
(1974) and Blandford & Rees (1974) are correct. The radio hotspots, lobes, and
bridges of classical double (FRII) radio sources are powered by two oppositely-
directed, highly collimated outflows from a compact object (probably a black
hole) that lies close to the center of the host galaxy or quasar (for an alternative
view, see, for example, Kundt 2000). The beam power, Lj, or energy per unit
time, impacts the ambient medium, and terminates in a very strong shock
near or at the radio hotspot; the radio hotspot is the direct result of this
interaction. The source size (distance between the two hotspots, or distance
between the core and each hotspot) increases with time as long as the beam
power is maintained by the compact object. The source also expands laterally
(perpendicular to the core-hotspot axis). Thus, over time, the length, width,
and radio surface brightness at different points within the radio emitting region
all evolve.

Second: most researchers agree that Scheuer’s dentist drill model (Scheuer
1982) provides an accurate description of the sources. Scheuer’s idea is that the
axis between the core and the hotspot does not maintain a fixed position. That
is, the position of the hotspot wanders a bit, so the overall rate of growth of the
source size is slower than the instantaneous hotspot velocity. This wandering
is similar to the wandering of a dentist drill on a tooth. The wandering may be
caused by precession of the black hole, or by some other physical process(es).
Whatever the cause of the wandering, there is strong evidence that the overall
rate of growth of the source is significantly less than the instantaneous velocity
of the hotspot (Scheuer 1982).

Third: most researchers in the field agree that a strong shock exists in the
immediate vicinity of the radio hotspot. Thus, we all agree that the position
of the hotspot moves forward with a speed that is much greater than the sound
speed of the ambient medium.

Fourth: we all agree on the set of equations that are valid at the “point of
contact” (i.e. the hotspot):

(e.g. Scheuer 1974; Blandford & Rees 1974; Norman et al. 1982; Bridle & Perley
1984; Begelman, Blandford, & Rees 1984; De Young 1986; Leahy 1991). Note
that, in most sources, NONE of these quantities can be empirically determined.
So, typically, we do not know the values of the beam power Lj, the cross
sectional area of the point of contact Ah, the jet velocity vj, the ambient gas
density na, or the pressure just behind the area of contact ph.

Fifth: Along the direction of the core-hotspot axis, there are two separate shock
systems in the dentist drill model, and each moves forward with a different
velocity. This occurs because of the wandering of the point of contact. Thus,
the instantaneous rate of growth of the source along the jet axis, vh, is typically
much larger than the average rate of growth of the source in this direction,
called the lobe propagation velocity vL (Scheuer 1982; Cox, Gull, & Scheuer
1991; Daly 1990, 1995). The lobe propagation velocity, vL, is the spatial and
temporal average of vh over the forward region (sometimes called the “lobe”
or the “head”) of the source.

Sixth: The following equations are valid over the forward region of the lobe
(along the direction of the jet axis) when the lobe is moving supersoni-
cally:

where pL is the lobe pressure, or average pressure of the full forward region
that is moving into the ambient medium in the direction of the jet axis; the
other symbols are defined above (e.g. De Young 1971; Daly 1990, 1994, 1995;
Falle 1991; Rawlings & Saunders 1991; Loken et al. 1992).

2.2 Where the Models Diverge

The primary differences between models has to do with the assumptions
adopted, and the approach taken. Key differences between models arise over
the following points. First: Does the model account for vL 6= vh? Given our cur-
rent understanding of these sources, this seems to be required by any model.
Second: Does the model assume that BOTH vL and vh are supersonic FOR
ALL FRIIs? Once it is acknowledged that vL < vh, the possibility that some
sources have vh supersonic, and vL sub- or transonic immediately arises. Third:
Does the model use the “direct” equations, equations (2) and (3) to describe
vL, or does the model follow a prescription to take some kind of spatial and

4



temporal average of equations (1) (which only apply to the point of contact),
to estimate vL? If some kind of averaging is carried out, a whole list of as-
sumptions related to how the averaging will be done must also be adopted,
and these assumptions must be reviewed.

Fourth: How does the model treat the lateral expansion of the bridge? (This
is the bridge expansion in the direction perpendicular to the jet axis.) Some
models treat this as a shock system (e.g. Daly 1990). Others treat this expan-
sion self-similarly (e.g. Falle 1991). And, in many models the point is simply
not addressed, and it is not clear what approach and assumptions are taken.

Fifth: Does the model include a detailed history of the relativistic electron
population, such as the models of Eilek & Shore (1989), Alexander and Leahy
(1987), Alexander (1987), Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens (1989), Wellman, Daly,
& Wan (1997a,b), and Blundell, Rawlings, & Willott (1999)? If so, is the ap-
proach realistic? What initial conditions are chosen, and are the initial condi-
tions empirically or theoretically determined?

Sixth: Does the model assume minimum energy conditions to determine the
magnetic field strength, B? Is this assumption a good one? How does this
assumption propagate through the theoretical calculations and predictions of
quantities to be compared with observations? Wellman, Daly, & Wan (1997a,b)
do not assume minimum energy conditions, and, in fact, find that the sources
are significantly offset (by a factor of about 4 or 5 in field strength) from
minimum energy conditions.

2.3 Discussion of a Few Specific Models

Here, a few specific models developed over the past decade will be reviewed.
The models are meant to be representative of the types of models being con-
sidered, but, because of space limitations, only a few models can be discussed.

The models seems to focus on different areas. Three main areas of focus may
be identified. These are: (1) Models that focus on properties of the relativistic
electron population. (2) Models that focus on radio source evolution through
the P - D diagram, where P is the total radio power, and D is the separation
between the two radio hotspots. And, (3) models that focus on the evolution of
the size, shape, and radio properties of the radio lobe and bridge of individual
sources.

Examples of models that focus on the properties of the relativistic electron
population are those of Eilek & Shore (1989), and Alexander (1987). Eilek &
Shore (1989) modelled the evolution of an FRII source with time including
the dynamical and energetic evolution of the source. A detailed analysis of the

5



evolution of the relativistic electrons is included. They find that a source with
a steady rate of energy input will be brightest (in the radio) at an age compa-
rable with the electron radiative lifetime, and will fade thereafter. Alexander
(1987) modelled the relativistic electron population in 3C234 in detail, includ-
ing acceleration, and adiabatic and radiative losses. The model was compared
in detail to multi-frequency observations (obtained at five frequencies). This
kind of modelling and comparison with observation can lead to a
deep understanding of the physical processes that determine the
radio properties of FRII sources. The source is in a cluster of galaxies.
If the ambient gas density can be estimated with X-ray data, any offset of
the magnetic field from minimum energy conditions can be determined (as
has been done by Carilli et al. 1991 for Cygnus A). This type of detailed
comparison between the model and the radio observations is quite
valuable.

Other models focus on the evolution of sources through the P-D plane. Com-
parisons of this type are statistical in nature; the evolution of a population of
sources through this diagram is investigated, and compared with the P-D dia-
gram for a large sample of sources. To be accurate, the large sample of sources
should be subdivided into FRIIa and FRIIb sources (discussed in §3), and into
radio galaxies and radio loud quasars. For example, Kaiser, Dennett-Thorpe,
& Alexander (1997) studied the evolution of sources through the P - D plane.
A detailed model of the evolution of sources was included, and source beam
powers ranging from 1045 erg/s to 1047 erg/s were used. The data points fill
the region between their upper and lower theoretical curve. Given the scatter
of points on the P-D diagram, and the many parameters that enter into the
model, it seems likely that just about any model would fit the data. Blundell
& Rawlings (1999) study the evolution of sources in the P-D diagram in a
detailed model with many parameters. They consider jet powers in the same
range as those considered by Kaiser, Dennett-Thorpe, & Alexander (1997).
Blundell, Rawlings, & Willott (1999) present results similar to those obtained
by Kaiser, Dennett-Thorpe, & Alexander (1997). A detailed evolution of the
relativistic electron population is included.

Other models focus on the temporal evolution of the size, shape, and radio
properties of the radio lobe and bridge of individual sources. For example,
Daly (1990) applied strong shock physics to determine the properties of the
radio lobe and bridge. The shape of the radio bridge, and other properties were
predicted; in later work, it was found that these predictions were accurate (see
§3.2). The same bridge shape was also predicted by Begelman & Cioffi (1989)
using an independent argument. If the radio lobe of a source moves
forward supersonically, this model provides an accurate description
of the shape and dynamical evolution of the radio source.

Falle (1991) obtained similarity solutions that describe the dynamical evolu-

6



tion of a supersonic source. His equation describing the growth of the source
along the jet axis is identical to that obtained by Daly (1990) using completely
different arguments. However, the similarity solution obtained by Falle (1991)
for the lateral growth of the source differs from that of Daly (1990) and Begel-
man & Cioffi (1989), and is inconsistent with observations (see §3.2). Falle
(1991) notes in his paper that a similarity solution may not provide an accu-
rate description of the lateral expansion of the source.

Cox, Gull, & Scheuer (1991) studied the evolution of a radio source using
the “dentist drill” model of a source. It is shown that the lobe propagation
velocity is lower than the hotspot velocity (as anticipated by Scheuer 1982).
The numerical code uses equations (1) that apply to the hotspot, allows the
hotspot to “wander,” and solves numerically for vL; the results obtained for
vL in this manner are in agreement with those predicted using the strong
shock physics model of Daly (1990), and the similarity solution of Falle (1991),
(which are identical) applied to the entire forward shock front.

Kaiser & Alexander (1997) study self-similar solutions for the radio bridge
and cocoon (of shocked ambient gas). As mentioned above, the self-similar
solution for the growth of the source along the jet axis is likely to be correct,
since it was obtained using independent approaches by Daly (1990) and Falle
(1991), and has been shown by Wellman, Daly, & Wan (1997a,b) to accurately
predict the properties of FRIIb radio sources. However, the self-similar solution
probably does not provide an accurate description of the lateral expansion of
the bridge, since the independent approaches of Begelman & Cioffi (1989) and
Daly (1990) yield identical results, which differ from those of Falle (1991),
and which have been shown to accurately predict the properties of the sources
(Wellman, Daly, & Wan 1997a,b).

3 Observational Constraints

Any model developed to describe FRII radio sources MUST address certain
observational constraints. At the present time, extensive, detailed, radio data
on many individual FRII sources is available, as is statistical information for
very large samples of sources. My philosophy is that a model should FIRST
be able to accurately reproduce the detailed properties of several individual
sources; only after this step should the model be applied and compared with
the statistical properties of a large sample. Otherwise, a model can reproduce
the statistical properties of a very large sample for all of the wrong reasons,
and may not be able to reproduce the observed characteristics of individual
sources, such as the shape, size, and radio properties across a given source.
In addition, great caution must be used when comparing statistical properties
to insure that a homogeneous sample is compiled, and does not include

7



sources that are governed by different physical processes. Statistical
results will change depending on whether the FULL population includes ALL
FRIIs, and whether galaxies and quasars are analyzed separately.

Given the great importance of the comparison between a model and the prop-
erties of individual sources, I will focus on some of the detailed radio obser-
vations that are invaluable in constraining models. For example, much can be
learned from detailed studies of the structure of radio bridges of FRII sources,
such as the studies of Leahy & Williams (1984), Alexander and Leahy (1987),
Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens (1989), and Liu, Pooley, & Riley (1992).

Leahy & Williams (1984) obtained VLA images of a complete sample of 39 3C
FRII sources. Sources with z < 0.5 were studied in detail, and have relatively
low power for FRII sources (powers in the range from about 1024.4 to 1027.4

W/Hz/sr for Ho = 100 km/s/Mpc). ALL of the sources were found to have
radio bridges, and many of the bridges are distorted. Given the diversity of the
radio bridge structure, Leahy & Williams (1984) defined 5 categories of
FRII sources based on the type of bridge distortion. They also defined
the axial ratio, and found that high power sources are longer and thinner than
low power sources.

Alexander & Leahy (1987) observed 21 3CR classical doubles (FRII sources)
at 4 frequencies at the VLA. The 178 MHz radio powers of the sources range
from 1025 to 1028 W/Hz/sr for Ho = 50 km/s/Mpc. They used the variation
in the radio spectrum to estimate the mean rate of growth of each source; this
is the lobe propagation velocity, vL. Alexander & Leahy (1987) found that
vL ∝ P 0.33±0.13, where P is the radio power. Similar results were obtained by
Daly (1995) using the sample of Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens (1989). This
relationship implies that more powerful sources grow faster.

It is interesting and significant that Alexander & Leahy (1987) find no corre-
lation between the overall rate of growth of a source vL, and the source size
(defined as the physical separation between the radio hotspots). This was, per-
haps, the first indication that the total time an AGN is on (producing beams
that power the growth of a source) is smaller for sources with larger velocities.
If more powerful sources grow faster, but are not larger (on average) than less
powerful sources, the more powerful sources must have shorter lifetimes.

Alexander & Leahy (1987) note the growth rate obtained using synchrotron
aging is a combination of the true rate of growth of the source vL and the
backflow velocity vbf : |vobs| = |vL|+ |vbf |. The authors note that their results,
combined with the results of Leahy & Williams (1984) suggest that backflow
is less important for higher power sources.

Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens (1989) report on observations obtained with Mer-
lin of 12 3C radio galaxies and 7 3C quasars; all of the sources have 178 MHz

8



radio powers greater than 1027 W/Hz/sr for Ho = 100 km/s/Mpc and qo = 0.
They detected complete bridges in 15 sources, and partial bridges in the other
sources. They confirmed the trend found by Leahy & Williams (1984), that
the bridges of more powerful sources are more elongated (that is, they have a
larger axial ratio) than the bridges of less powerful FRII sources.

Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens (1989) also find that the radio galaxies and radio
loud quasars in their sample have different bridge structure, and the difference
is probably not due to projection effects alone. Note that this implies that it
is important to distinguish between radio galaxies and radio loud quasars in
studies.

Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens (1989) also find that radio galaxies with P178 >
1027 W/Hz/sr (for Ho = 100 km/s/Mpc) all have a “cigar-like” bridge shape.
The radio bridges of these sources have a very regular “cigar-like”
shape, with few bridge distortions, and they all correspond to a
single type, given the bridge types defined by Leahy & Williams
(1984). Thus, all of the sources are likely to be governed by the same physical
processes, and, perhaps can all be explained by a single model for radio source
development. For example, the authors note that backflow is probably not
important in these sources.

Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens (1989) also find, for high power sources, most of
the radio power comes from the hotspots/lobe region, and not from the radio
bridge (see figure 22 in their paper). Thus, in terms of the evolution of the radio
power of the source with time, losses in the bridge will not significantly affect
the total radio power of these sources, since most of the power is generated
in the forward region of the source. In addition, the authors find that there is
a correlation between bridge power and total power, so the radio power of a
source is not likely to undergo large variations over the source lifetime.

3.1 What Does All This Mean?

As demonstrated above, a significant and ample body of data about the prop-
erties of the radio bridges of individual FRII sources exists. This information
should be used to constrain models of FRII sources.

For example, modellers should try to constrain the models with existing de-
tailed information on radio bridges, such as the radio surface brightness
and bridge width as a function of position along the bridge. This has
been done by some authors, such as Eilek & Shore (1989), Alexander (1987),
and Wellman, Daly, & Wan (1997a,b), but has not been addressed by others.

The observational results suggest that the physics of lower power FRIIs (which

9



typically show highly distorted radio bridges), and higher power FRIIs (which,
especially radio galaxies, typically show smooth, regular, cigar-like radio bridges)
may be different. In particular, the equations used by modellers to describe the
sources may only apply to some fraction of the sources. If some physical pro-
cesses are different for high- and low-power FRIIs (as indicated empirically)
then different models should be developed to describe the different types of
FRII sources, since one set of equations may not describe all types of sources.
For example, as already suggested by Leahy & Williams (1984) and Leahy,
Muxlow, & Stephens (1989), the lower power sources may have significantly
more backflow than the higher power sources.

An intriguing possibility is that in the higher power sources (those with 178
MHz radio power P178 > 3h−2×1026 W/Hz/sr for Ho = 100 h km/s/kpc) have
a lobe propagation velocity and a hotspot velocity that are both supersonic,
while for the lower power FRIIs the hotspot velocity is supersonic while the
lobe propagation velocity is subsonic (or transonic). Thus, the physics of the
sources may be different. Note that this type of explanation may go hand in
hand with that proposed by Leahy & Williams (1984) and Leahy, Muxlow, &
Stephens (1989), and would serve to explain why the backflow properties of
high- and low-power FRIIs may be different.

Because of the fundamental difference in the radio bridge struc-
ture for FRIIs with high and low radio power, we should really talk
about 2 categories of FRII sources: FRIIa sources are those with
distorted radio bridges, and FRIIb sources are those with regular,
well-behaved, cigar-like bridges. Since bridge distortion is strongly cor-
related with radio power, this can also be defined in terms of radio power.
Roughly, FRIIa sources have 178 MHz radio powers less than about
3h−2 × 1026 W/Hz/sr for Ho = 100 h km/s/Mpc, and FRIIb sources
have 178 MHz radio powers greater than about 3h−2×1026 W/Hz/sr.

To be accurate, all analyses of FRII sources, especially statistical compar-
isons between a model and the data, should always split the radio data into
these two power ranges before comparing theoretical predictions with obser-
vations. This simply follows from the fact that it is very unlikely that a single
model formalism will be able to explain both types of sources. A split into
radio galaxies and radio loud quasars would further clarify how well model
predictions compare with observations.

3.2 The Power of the Strong Shock Physics Model

The strong shock physics model of FRIIb radio sources is powerful because
it allows the fundamental physical variables that describe the radio

10



source and its environment to be determined using radio observa-
tions. The model is similar to many other models proposed to describe FRII
radio sources. For example, as mentioned earlier, the results of the strong shock
physics model for the growth of the source along the jet axis are identical to
those of Falle (1991), and the results of the strong shock physics model for the
growth of the source in the lateral direction are identical to those of Begelman
& Cioffi (1989). The model is presented by Daly (1990) and is developed and
applied by Daly (1994,1995), Wellman, Daly, & Wan (1997a,b), Wan & Daly
(1998a,b), Guerra & Daly (1998), Wan, Daly, & Guerra (2000), and Guerra,
Daly, & Wan (2000).

Some characteristics of the model will be described here.

3.2.1 The Shape of the Radio Bridge

The strong shock physics model and the model of Begelman & Cioffi (1989)
independently predicted that the width aL of the radio bridge (perpendicular
to the core-hotspot line) would vary with distance x from the radio hotspot
as aL ∝ √

x up to some distance xb from the hotspot. At this distance xb from
the hotspot a break is predicted, and the bridge width should remain roughly
constant for larger x (see the detailed discussion by Wellman, Daly, & Wan
1997a,b).

The strong shock physics model was only applied to FRIIb sources, for the
reasons described in the previous section. The model is designed to describe
FRII sources with regular bridge shape, such as the FRIIb sources, in which
both vL and vh are supersonic. To test the prediction, a sample of FRIIb
sources with sufficient bridge data was compiled. All FRIIb sources with radio
bridge information were taken from the samples of Leahy, Muxlow, & Stephens
(1989) and Liu, Pooley, & Riley (1992). This yielded a sample of 14 radio
galaxies and 8 radio loud quasars. Only sources with sizes greater than 20
kpc were included (so the sources would all have a significant radio bridge to
study). Amazingly, the radio bridge width was found to vary as aL ∝ x0.49±0.01

(Wellman, Daly, & Wan 1997a), where approximately 30 radio bridges were
used (for many sources we were able to use both radio bridges, and in some
sources, we could only use the radio bridge on one side of the source) and
approximately 6 points along the bridge were used for each source. In many of
the sources the break location was determined. For these, sources, the location
of the break can be used to determine the Mach number with which the lobe
is propagating into the ambient gas.

3.2.2 The Radio Surface Brightness Profile

The radio surface brightness from the radio hotspot to the radio core, or host
galaxy center, was studied. It was found the the radio surface brightness could
be very accurately predicted by assuming the lobe width and radio power
of a given source are roughly constant over time, and that adiabatic losses
dominate at low radio frequency. That is, the radio power at any position
x can be accurately predicted by assuming the radio power was identical to
that currently seen at the radio lobe (forward region of the radio bridge) and
decreased due to adiabatic expansion in the lateral direction by an amount
given by the width at that point and the width currently seen at the lobe.
There is no indication that the radio power of a given radio source
decreases with time.

This suggests a very simple model for these very powerful FRIIb sources: the
radio power and size of the radio emitting region near the forward edge of the
radio bridge are roughly constant over the source lifetime, and the decrease in
radio surface brightness across the source is due to adiabatic expansion. The
fact that the radio surface brightness across the source can be so accurately
predicted suggests that backflow of relativistic plasma within the bridge, and
particle re-acceleration within the bridge, are not significant.

3.2.3 The Mach Number of Lobe Advance

The Shape of a radio bridge of an FRIIb source can be used to estimate the
Mach Number, M, of lobe advance. The ratio of lobe pressure to ambient gas
pressure is determined by the Mach number: PL/Pa ' 2 M2. As mentioned
above, many sources in our sample exhibit a break in radio bridge shape. The
location and width of this break may be used to estimate the Mach number
with which the radio lobe propagates into the ambient gas. Values of M were
obtained for about 16 radio bridges (Wellman, Daly, & Wan 1997a), and the
values of M range from about 2.5 to 10. For M ranging from 2.5 to 10,
the pressure ratio PL/Pa ranges from about 10 to 200.

total pressure in the lobe is then

3.2.6 The Velocity of Lobe Propagation

The velocity of lobe propagation was estimated using a synchrotron and in-

propagation velocities for the Liu, Pooley, & Riley (1992) sources
are significantly less than the hotspot velocities obtained by Liu,
Pooley, & Riley 1992. This echos comments made earlier in this paper:
there are many reasons to expect the lobe propagation velocity to be less than
the hotspot velocity, and this is exactly what was found.

The velocities of lobe propagation obtained range from about 2× 103 km/s to
about 2×104 km/s. They are similar for radio galaxies and radio loud quasars,
and there is no strong dependence on source size.

3.2.9 FRIIb Radio Sources Lie in Clusters of Galaxies

The FRIIb radio sources studied lie in environments with ambient gas pres-
sures, ambient gas densities, and ambient gas temperatures that are similar to
low-redshift clusters of galaxies. Thus, these high-power FRII sources (FRIIb
sources) most likely lie in clusters of galaxies, though they have redshifts all
the way to a redshift of 2! The symmetry of the sources, and the composite
density profile obtained for the sources argue that they lie within the central
core of the cluster, and may be a giant elliptical galaxy located very close to
core of the X-ray gas.

For the radio galaxies in this sample, the beam power increases weakly with
